speechtext:

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF PUBLIC BILLS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
May I refer to the practice which has arisen in recent years with regard to the introduction and first reading of public bills. On today's order paper there are listed some 120 bills for introduction by private members. It was not practical or possible for the Chair to review the provisions of each of those bills. May I therefore suggest to the House that we adopt the procedure which was agreed upon in recent sessions, namely, that we proceed to the introduction and first reading of those bills so that each may be scrutinized between now and its being called for second reading in order to allow the Chair to consider whether there is any defect in the bills in respect of the practices and usages of the House.
I suggest that by unanimous consent all the public bills listed in the names of private members for introduction on today's order paper be deemed to have been introduced, given first reading and ordered to be printed, and to stand for second reading at the next sitting of the House, subject of course to a subsequent examination as to the regularity of each bill. Is the procedure to which I have referred agreed to by the House?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance when he will be publishing or making public the agenda for the proposed meeting between himself and the provincial treasurers or ministers of finance. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I would be prepared to publish that agenda when I am satisfied that the provinces are willing to have that done and have agreed to the various items on the agenda. Speaking in terms of my own priorities for discussion, I would want a thorough canvassing of the economic situation of the country, of the fiscal position of the federal government as we see it, and of the provincial governments as they anticipate those positions to be during the course of the calendar year and next fiscal year. speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, January 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. J. Blais for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Crouse (p. 245).

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to continue my speech on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne I wish, first of all, to extend my congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, on your re-election as Speaker of this House. You have distinguished yourself in this position in the last two parliaments. You have shown courage and dedication by agreeing to accept this high office again. Whatever the difficulties of this parliament, and judging by the breakdown of the numbers in each party there will be many, your wisdom and firm hand will maintain the dignity and decorum of the House.
I also want to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) on his election to the position of Deputy Speaker. I have confidence in him and count him as a friend. We spent several weeks together at an Interparliamentary Union conference in 1969. I believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the House have shown real wisdom in appointing him Deputy Speaker. It will require all the sagacity, good will, and humour that the Chair can muster to make this a productive House.
I consider it a great honour to be re-elected to represent Algoma in the House of Commons and I thank my constituents for this responsibility and the opportunity to serve them. Election campaigns bring a person in to close contact with many people in a compressed time frame, they are more effective than any other methods I know of. The excitement and celebration of winning an election campaign can only be justified by hard work both in this chamber and in the constituency.
I congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply. They have youth, vigour, and eloquence in both our

official languages and show great promise of becoming competent Members of Parliament.
I am especially pleased that the hon. member for Nipiss-ing (Mr. Blais) was chosen because he comes from northern Ontario. We are often concerned that not enough attention is paid to northern Ontario. Part of this problem stems from the fact that we are from a "have-not" area of a "have" province. We have many problems similar to those of the western and eastern provinces, such as high transportation costs, declining population and slow economic growth. However, because we are part of a wealthy province our needs are not fully recognized either at the provincial or federal level in many instances.
This is brought home only too forcefully in the proposals of the Representation Commissioner which were published on December 27, 1972. These proposals suggest that there will be two fewer Members of Parliament to represent northern Ontario in the House of Commons. This means that ridings which are already too large will be larger. Members who now divide their time as carefully and fairly as possible between dozens of communities will have to add many more towns and villages. City Members of Parliament do not fully appreciate how much the smaller communities depend on their Member of Parliament to help them in making approaches to government with a maze of what might be considered small problems. In the totality of government expenditures they may be relatively small problems, but for these communities they are big and important matters concerning their progress and development. When I see the ridings enlarged in northern Ontario I am not concerned so much about the extra miles I will have to travel as with the fact that the members for such enlarged ridings will have relatively less time for each community. I am also concerned that the total impact of members from northern Ontario will be made by 10 members instead of the present 12. It seems to me that the Representation Commissioner in the final determination should consider these facts before reducing the total number of members in the north.
An important step was taken in 1969 to rectify the discrepancy between the north and south by the establishment of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the designation of northern Ontario as an area where special assistance was available. It is strange that the provincial government, with all its wealth and power, does not have special assistance available to the slow growth areas of the north.
The DREE program has been criticized by many during the recent election campaign as being ineffective. I want to see the program strengthened, improved and made more flexible. I think that the minimum size for enterprises which can qualify for incentive grants should be reduced. I am pleased to see that the department is to be decentralized as this should bring it closer to the areas to be served. It will make personal consultation and discussion possible.
I was pleased to read in the Speech from the Throne as well that there will be improved assistance to strengthen management and consulting services for small businesses along with improved access to financing facilities. It is a
January 15, 1973

constant problem for the small businesses in my riding to secure financing for their enterprises. It seems there should be increased management services available to recipients of DREE grants to ensure that these companies not only meet the equity and other requirements of the act and regulations to qualify for a grant, but also to continue to keep the project operating viably.
I would like to see DREE grants available to the tourist industry as well. In many areas of Canada which are now designated for these grants, such as northern Ontario, we have all the natural beauty for tourism. We have, in the Algoma riding alone, hundreds of miles of shoreline on Lake Huron and Lake Superior as well as a multitude of lakes and streams. However, the financial wherewithal is lacking to develop our tourist industry fully. The Speech from the Throne outlines help for the tourist industry. I hope this is help which will be beneficial at the local level and not just some national survey system which will have little effect.
I am looking forward with interest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introducing changes to extend and improve the Industrial Development Bank. This will be good news for the small businessmen who in the past have found it a hard-nosed organization with high interest rates and closed-end mortgages in which no one could get very interested. The rates should be lowered and the pay-off arrangement should be open-ended. I am told by businessmen in my riding that the funds available and the interest charged by the bank in making loans have increased in the past several months. This is encouraging. When the amendments are introduced I hope they will contain provisions to make the terms of the loans more attractive.
The Speech from the Throne proposes that the federal government will meet with the provinces to examine the impact of freight rates on economic development and consumer prices. There can be little doubt what the results of this examination will show. It will show that freight rates and transportation costs raise consumer prices in northern Ontario and inhibit economic development. The DREE program of incentive grants is designed to be a stimulus to overcome this effect on economic development, but it does not fully compensate for the transportation costs. The costs of transportation are likewise detrimental to consumer prices in the Algoma riding. This meeting of federal and provincial governments should produce a solution to this problem which is as old as confederation itself.
I suggest that when these discussions are held with the province of Ontario they be held in northern Ontario. We are the people who suffer from the high freight rates. We are the people most concerned in this province. The good will of both the federal and provincial governments in these discussions could be demonstrated by holding these meetings in northern Ontario.
The Speech from the Throne gives an outline of the measures to provide jobs on a direct employment basis to counteract the unemployment problem. These include the local initiatives program, the on-the-job-training program, direct employment by the federal government on labourintensive projects and the winter capital projects fund.
I believe that the winter capital projects fund will be a most beneficial program to municipalities. It will be a
The Address-Mr. Foster
loan fund of $350 million for community projects. As I understand the program, it will operate for two and a half years. One half of the on-site labour costs will be forgiven during the summer months and all of the labour costs forgiven during the winter months. The advantage to the local municipality is that it provides a source of loan funds in which labour costs are forgiven. However, all the construction does not have to be undertaken during the difficult winter months, although there is additional incentive if it is carried out then. I hope the Minister of Finance will be sending the information on this program in the very near future to the provincial governments who will administer it. There is interest in this program, but detailed information is just not available.
Likewise, with the local initiatives program the approvals are coming through so late this year that the total impact of the program is reduced. Henceforth, the program should be started with the approval of projects so that work can begin in November and, where projects are not completed by May 31, extensions should be made.
The Speech from the Throne outlines several measures concerning our social policy. The relationship between social aid, unemployment insurance and work in our society is one Of the most complex because it involves all levels of government, the private sector of our economy and a person's ability to work and get a job. It is proposed that the blind, disabled and aged will receive an equitable guaranteed annual income, that there will be an incentive to work built into our social welfare system and a more equitable relationship between those who require social aid and those who work at the minimum wage level. There has been increasing criticism of these problems recently in my constituency. Good co-ordination between the welfare board and community local initiative programs has been beneficial in some areas of Algoma. However, this has only been helpful in the winter months. I hope these proposals contained in the Speech from the Throne will be useful in building a system which will utilize the employable recipient of welfare or unemployment insurance benefits for worth-while community projects when no work in the private sector of our economy is available.
The speech also outlines the intention of the government to increase the benefits of old age pensioners. This will be welcome news to the pensioners in my constituency. I am surprised that more people are not aware of the automatic escalator clause in the old age pensions which we passed last spring after the budget, it is my understanding that the basic old age security pension is now raised to $86.51 per month. The maximum benefit under the guaranteed income supplement and old age security is now $156.75 per month for a single pensioner and $297 per month for a couple. The Minister of Finance should immediately introduce the bill to increase the additional exemption for old age pensioners to $1,000. I have received many letters from constituents requesting that this provision of last June's budget be implemented.
We have seen some interesting politicking going on in the House this week. We see the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) hungry for power, ready to move any motion and pursue any strategy to achieve it. We have seen "Prince George" of Hastings try to adjourn the

January 15, 1973
The Address-Mr. Hellyer
debate on the Speech from the Throne before the fundamental constitutional vote of confidence in the government was taken. I am glad to see that the other parties in the House are not buying this nonsense. It is interesting that the government won that vote 154 to 104, which is a larger majority than many of the votes in the last parliament. I do not believe the people of this country want this kind of politicking. I do not believe the people of this country want another election. I have talked in my constituency to voters from all political parties and they say: get on with the job of governing; bring in legislation to build a better economy and to build a better society, a better Canada.

speechtext: This should be our goal this session, utilizing the outline of legislation contained in the Speech from the Throne to ensure that the real winners as a result of our efforts are the Canadian people.

speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say how pleased I am that you have been unanimously chosen to preside over us once again. As your seatmate during part of the last parliament, I came to know your human qualities of understanding and compassion as well as your more public characteristics of a sense of justice and unfailing good humour. In the performance of your duties I know you will be supported and encouraged by your lovely and gracious wife.

speechtext:
I should like to extend my congratulations also to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) who will act as your deputy. Few members of this House are as universally regarded with both respect and affection as he.

I also wish to congratulate the hon. members for Nipiss-ing and Lachine (Messrs. Blais and Blaker) on their being elected to the House of Commons, and on having had the honour of being chosen mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne which task they fulfilled with eloquence. They are fortunate in being able to speak with such ease both official languages of our country. I wish them much success in their parliamentary career.

Although the quality of this debate has been unusually high, Mr. Speaker, I must say I was disappointed in the speeches made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). Fairly interpreted, their speeches have indicated that they have learned nothing from the election results. The people have spoken but the message has not been received by the government. The big three, now augmented by the incarnation of the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to the big four, have not got the message. They did not listen to their colleagues in cabinet; they

largely ignored the warnings of caucus; they totally ignored the most important policy decisions of the Liberal party and now they demonstrate by their attitude and by their intemperate language that the people, too, count for nothing.
Bilingualism was not a big issue in the election. It was important in the Ottawa area because the pledges given by Prime Minister Pearson and then by the present Prime Minister were not honoured. This created an atmosphere of suspicion and mistrust which was bound to be reflected in the vote. But in so far as the rest of the country is concerned, the issues were far more complex and represented, for the most part, a rejection of governmental incompetence and bungling in economic matters. This government failed to solve the ordinary issues of jobs and prices and housing as they affected many citizens, and the vote said so. It was an amalgam of unemployment, inflation, the abuse of unemployment insurance, the failure to take realistic steps to increase Canadian participation in the ownership and development of our own industries and resources, questionable LIP and OFY grants, failure to alleviate regional disparity, and a generally makeshift and amateurish approach to the solution of economic problems that destroyed the credibility of the government and its leaders.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The unemployment rate in Canada is too high. It is the worst of any industrialized country in the western world. This is a shameful situation, and, and as one United States economist said in Toronto a few weeks ago, it is totally unacceptable-he could not understand how it could be tolerated. His view was typical of the view held by others. A couple of years ago when I travelled around the world talking to some of the best economists, labour leaders and bankers, I was asked from time to time what the unemployment rate was in Canada. My answer was received by them with disbelief. In several instances, the person to whom I was talking asked: how could any democratic government survive with an unemployment rate as high as that?
We do not need United States economists or others to tell us about unemployment. We know it is a totally unsatisfactory situation. We know it is totally unacceptable to many Canadians and that something must be done about it. On Sunday I interviewed a number of constituents who were passionately-and in some cases desperately-seeking work at a living wage. The fact that they cannot find employment at a living wage underlines the contention that our unemployment rate is the number one indicator of gross incompetence. It is also the number one indicator of moral failure. When we have such a high unemployment rate, is it not a strange anomaly that there are, at the same time in Canada, tens of thousands of unfilled jobs? Many reasons are cited for this paradox. Some suggest it is because the unemployed do not have the proper qualifications for the jobs being offered. Close scrutiny indicates this is not normally the case. It is also suggested that many unemployed persons do not really want to find work. While this may be true of a small minority, a more credible and accurate explanation lies in the fact that in many cases the wages being offered are not sufficient to live on, and that in tens of thousands of
January 15, 1973

cases the relative advantage of working as against drawing unemployment insurance or welfare provides no incentive. Many individuals are financially better off not to work-or at least not to work full time.
The net result is business and moral chaos. Dress and garment manufacturers cannot hire needleworkers because potential employees can make more on unemployment insurance while doing piecework at home for cash. Tobacco growers could not get enough help to harvest the crop without hiring illegally, under assumed names, young people who were already in receipt of unemployment insurance. Tomato growers could not hire students at $20 a day to harvest their crops. Florists cannot hire workers to tend their greenhouses. Farmers are selling dairy herds because they cannot compete with unemployment insurance. These are some of the symptoms of distortions in our economy, Mr. Speaker. The root causes are deeper. Since 1970 there has been inadequate demand to provide enough jobs for everyone. The big powerful companies and their equally powerful unions have used their monopolistic or oligopolistic power to their own advantage and to the detriment of the weak. Small businesses and non-union labour have been unable to keep up. They, along with the old age pensioners and others living on fixed incomes, have been squeezed unmercifully. The maldistribution of income both regionally and vertically between citizens not only remains but has been exacerbated. Some people were so naive as to believe that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion would achieve miracles. But with its subjective approach to decision making, how could it hope to succeed.
My makeshift lectern, Mr. Speaker, consists of nothing but press releases and reports from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion telling us how much money it has spent and how many jobs it has created, or so we are told. But the jobs have evaporated. In December 1968 there were 152,000 unemployed persons seeking work in Quebec. In December 1972 there were 206,000 unemployed persons seeking work in Quebec, 54,000 more unemployed people in that province than when the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was established. Hundreds of millions of dollars down the drain, and for what?
In some cases money was given to businesses to do what they had planned to do in any event. In other cases, the departmental assistance merely resulted in moving unemployment from one part of the country to another at the taxpayers' expense. In these circumstances, how dare the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) say that the criticism levelled at him and his former department was based on anything other than gross incompetence.
At the same time that the minister was doing his inadequate best to create a few new jobs through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the government wiped out a larger number of jobs with its restrictive monetary policy. It was this schizophrenic approach to economic policy which Eric Kierans, and others, could not stomach. The shortage of aggregate demand caused by the tight money policy persists to this moment in spite of the government's best efforts. This is not news. No reliable forecaster has suggested that full employment was
The Address-Mr. Hellyer
just around the corner. No government spokesman has been so bold as to suggest that it is. But in spite of this, the government is still running a crisis operation without benefit of long-term planning.
As long ago as last June, the provincial premiers warned that policies to provide additional job opportunities would have to be launched at once to be effective in the winter months. Yet, notwithstanding this unanimous warning, the government procrastinated. Once again its makeshift programs were too late. The LIP program and the training on the job program were too late for efficient administration. The result is waste of precious funds, Mr. Speaker; inefficient, frustrating waste. I was interested to note that the Liberal speaker who preceded me agreed with my analysis.
On the more positive side, Mr. Speaker, it is somewhat encouraging to see the government's new-found interest in small business. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) reminds us that 60 per cent of the Canadian labour force is working for establishments having the essential characteristics of a small business. Under the circumstances, one might wonder why this sector has been so badly neglected until now.
The package of assistance outlined by the minister is quite impressive on paper. I hope it will produce results. Anyone who is experienced in small business is entitled to be a bit sceptical, however. It would take a tremendous boost to compensate small business for the hurdles which have been placed in its way. Our tax laws, especially death duties, discourage entrepreneurship. Our chartered banks are unduly concerned with potential losses from small business and consequently adequate financing is not readily available in many cases. And in this context, an uneven monetary policy and periodic reliance on monetary restriction have put thousands of small businesses into bankruptcy unnecessarily. On top of this, several levels of government are driving small businessmen up the proverbial wall with the number and complexity of laws and the paper work accompanying them.

The lack of encouragement for Canadian small business and the constant harassment of officialdom has resulted in the sale of many businesses to foreign owners. But he did not explain how the present trend would be reversed. He did not say how Canadians would be encouraged to save more so that they could participate more fully in the ownership of Canadian resources and industry. He did not promise that the government would curtail its appetite for new programs. He did not explain how the combined effects of confiscatory tax laws and inflation would be overcome.
The consequences of the combined effects of taxation and inflation on savings are not well understood. Let us take last year's Canada Savings Bonds as a case in point. The coupon rate for the first year is 5.5 per cent. From that must be deducted the inflation for the year, namely 5.1 per cent. That leaves a net return before tax of four-tenths of one per cent. Now if a taxpayer had a 30 per cent tax rate he would have to pay 30 per cent tax, not on the four-tenths of one per cent but on 51 per cent. That would be 1.65 per cent.
The net result is that anyone with a tax rate of 30 per cent who bought Canada Savings Bonds in 1972 and held them for one year only would not only be lending the government money with no return but would actually get back H per cent less purchasing power than he had at the outset. Only if he held the savings bond until maturity, and assuming that inflation will not rise above its present level, would the investor break even. In 1984, the poor sucker would get his money back without loss, once again, assuming that he did not have to pay to get his income tax forms and other accounting done for him. A grateful government would have the use of the taxpayer s money for 12 years without cost.
Unfortunately many other Canadian investments are equally discouraging. Many investors are hard pressed to place their savings where the purchasing power at the end of the year, after tax and inflation, will be as great as it

was on New Year's day. Is this the climate of opportunity that will encourage Canadians to scrimp and save in order to invest in their own future? I doubt it. It is hardly a healthy climate for business of any kind, small or large.
As important as inflation is for the investor or potential investor, it is 10 times more important for people at the bottom end of the income scale who cannot afford to live, let alone invest. Prices are going up-up-up. There has been a total failure on the part of the government to cope. The 5.1 per cent increase in the consumer price index in 1972 is the largest increase in 22 years. The Canadian experience has become, as one OECD economist put it, "a classic example" of what to avoid in fighting inflation.
In human terms, inflation spells tragedy. A case which came to my attention Saturday is typical of many I know. A constituent, a married man with two children, one aged 11 the other an infant, earns $4,900 a year. This leaves him $80 a week, net, in his pay envelope. He pays $35 a week rent plus $5 a week for coal. That leaves $40 weekly for a family of four. The wife requires special medication costing $15 weekly, leaving $25 for food, clothing and all other necessities. Last week she did not have $6 to pay the hydro bill and was threatened with having the service disconnected. When this man looks at some of the makeshift government programs on which his money is spent, he is full of resentment. Can you blame him, Mr. Speaker? How is a family going to survive under such circumstances? It is a desperate situation. Something must be done, now, to alleviate the suffering, both physical and psychological. A lengthy investigation into food prices will not satisfy this family, Mr. Speaker. They want action now.
Hear, hear!

Although the nature of our cost-push inflation is not yet admitted by all economists, the consensus is shifting. The threadbare orthodoxies which have governed official thinking are coming into disrepute. A total revision in thinking is necessary to avoid total catastrophe. The ability of the strong to exploit the weak must be curbed. A fairer distribution of income is essential to offset the distortions created by monopoly power in the so-called market place. A system under which a construction union can get a 35.7 per cent increase in 18 months while the minimum wage in nine of the 10 provinces is less than $2 must be re-examined, not after a royal commission or a task force has studied the problem to death, but now.
In summation, then, Mr. Speaker, the present situation will not wash. We have the highest unemployment rate in the western world while tens of thousands of jobs go unfilled. Confiscatory tax rates discourage savings and encourage sell-out to foreigners. Makeshift programs that result in frustration and waste, distort priorities while undermining accepted values of prudence and administration. Some people have never had it so good while the underprivileged and disadvantaged are desperate. Rising prices are causing real hardship and eroding the savings of innocent and helpless citizens.

The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said in Toronto last week that members of this party would vote for the Communist manifesto in order to gain power. He is wrong, Mr. Speaker. We would not even vote for the Regina manifesto in order to gain power.

When the vote is taken tonight, Mr. Speaker, I hope that all those members of this honourable House who really believe in their hearts that action is the handmaid of compassion will vote for the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with all the other honourable members of this House in saying how pleased I am to see you installed again as the Speaker of this Chamber. For you the burdens of office are particularly heavy, but we are all reassured that because you preside here our deliberations will be more orderly and, hopefully, more beneficial to those who sent us here. As well, I am personally very delighted with the choice of our new Deputy Speaker, a man who has the good reputation for both graciousness and fairness. I also know him to be a very hospitable person. This I discovered during a visit to Halifax in the summer of 1971 when I attended in that city an area conference of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association.
I also wish to commend the hon. members who moved and seconded the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. The excellent quality of their speeches has set a high standard for this debate.
As one who comes from northwestern Ontario, which is a developing region of Canada, I note with considerable satisfaction in the Speech from the Throne that in the area of economic policy the government remains committed to a program of regional economic expansion. Because of federal government assistance particularly since 1968, much has been achieved in this region which I am honoured to represent. That, of course, is quite contrary to what was just expressed by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). But we all recognize that a great deal more remains to be done. It was for that reason that I sought re-election, and it was for that reason that the electors in my contituency sent me here for another term. Indeed, I am most honoured to represent the people who live in that important area of Canada.
We in northwestern Ontario will be most interested to learn from the government how decentralizing the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and
The Address-Mr. Penner
extending and improving the Industrial Development Bank will assist us in lessening the continual economic disparity which exists between us and the more affluent regions of Canada. We have every intention of sharing in the good life that Canada has to offer, and we will work very hard to accomplish this goal.
The people who live in northwestern Ontario share to some considerable degree the kinds of grievances which are often expressed by those who come from western Canada. Our region belongs to neither the east nor the west, but is is the vital land bridge between the two. In common with those who come from the west, we know that the present freight rate system works against us. Because of high freight rates, the goods that we require in northwestern Ontario cost us more than the price paid by other Canadians. The development of secondary industry is discouraged because of the high cost of getting our products to markets. Meanwhile, Toronto and district are choking in their own growth, but we remain underdeveloped and underpopulated. It often seems to us that if the gluttonous south has had too much of highway building, airport development and expansion of housing, then why not let the people there look towards the mid-north where we desperately need all of these things and, of course, much more besides?
We in northwestern Ontario welcome the promised conference to examine the impact of freight rates on economic development. I would just remind the government, Sir, that although we are part of the great province of Ontario, northern Ontario is also a distinct geographic and economic region of Canada. We will therefore insist very strongly on having regional representation at one or more of these meetings which will consider the economic impact of the present freight rate structure.
We in northwestern Ontario are just as concerned about national unity as are Canadians anywhere else, but for us the question of national unity has little to do with language. It has, however, a great deal to do with the equality of opportunity and the availability of services which are considered essential by most other Canadians. In our region, we speak many different languages, including English and French, but we speak with one voice, we speak in unison, when it comes to asking for what most other Canadians take for granted, namely, an adequate level of health services throughout the region, decent housing, hydro electric power at the rate paid by our fellow citizens elsewhere, and adequate accommodation for our senior citizens so that they do not have to go hundreds of miles from where they lived and worked. We ask as well for reasonably prompt mail service; good, clear, television reception with a choice of channels; a say in some of the decisions which directly affect us; and more job opportunities for our young people, which, undoubtedly can be brought about if we would do more of the processing of our natural resources on the site before we send them south or export them abroad.
Later in my remarks I hope to say more on the subject of resource development, but now I would like to make a brief comment about television in our area. Many of our communities still have very poor or no television reception at all. It is the CBC's stated objective to extend its

The Address-Mr. Penner
television and radio service to every community of 500 persons or more. The government has authorized the CBC to extend its services in a comprehensive fashion, but we in northwestern Ontario feel that there is a great deal of foot dragging by the Corporation. The CBC loves to complain about its restricted budget, and yet there always seems to be money to send large crews abroad to cover sports extravaganzas such as the Olympics. Incidentally, the Olympics are one international sideshow which I hope does not come to Canada. The CBC has no difficulty in finding a large sum of money to produce an abortive drama series like the "Whiteoaks of Jalna"; the capital budget is never so restricted as to prevent the CBC from building huge broadcasting cathedrals to house the modern day priests of culture and communication. We in northwestern Ontario question the priorities of the CBC. We believe that the corporation is inefficient and wasteful, and we object to the CBC's expensive pampering to the prissy, over-sophisticated tastes of a mere handful of Canadians. It would certainly be refreshing if this corporation could rediscover the meaning and value of popular entertainment.
To go to another topic, let me say that during the recent election campaign many residents of northwestern Ontario raised the question with me and other candidates about the ownership of land in Canada by aliens or nonresidents. I hasten here to define the meaning of non-resident in this context. By non-resident is meant an individual who does not have Canadian citizenship or landed immigrant status. The throne speech refers to measures dealing with the sale of land to foreigners. What is needed now is a moratorium on the sale or lease of private or public land to aliens until such time as suitable legislation can be prepared and enacted. The moratorium ought to take effect immediately.
I subscribe to the view of those who argue that Crown land, whether in the federal or provincial jurisdiction, should not be sold under any circumstances. Further, Crown land should not be leased to non-residents. Where non-residents now own land in Canada, they should be subject to double taxation, and certain areas of high recreational potential must be expropriated and returned to public ownership.
The Speech from the Throne mentions that steps will be taken to assist in the development of the tourist industry in Canada. One of the ways in which this can be done is to reduce the number of non-resident owners of recreational land in a tourist region. Since one of the main objectives in tourism is to maximize profits, we should consider the relative economic benefits of two groups of tourists. The first, and the largest group, consists of true tourists, those who are travelling through an area, eating in restaurants, staying at camps, campsites or motels, and possibly paying admission to certain attractions. The second type of tourist is the non-resident owner who makes directly for his or her own private spot of seclusion and remains there. As a group, the non-resident owners are smaller and much less economically important than the travelling visitor or "guest" type of tourist.
To help attract even more of these travelling tourists, governments should be doing much more. They should become much more active in the establishment and the
running of local family-centred summer and winter tourist facilities. No subsidies should be given for the operation of tourist facilities by non-residents. Both levels of government should determine the requirements of the private tourist industry to help meet the growing pressures on facilities from the rapid increase in tourist traffic from the United States. Again, no subsidies should be given to non-resident tourist industry operators.
Northwestern Ontario is a vast area, and at present tourists are permitted to wander almost at will and without the help of qualified guides. This, of course, has reduced suitable employment for many of our native people and also results in many of these tourists becoming lost in the bush and sometimes dying there. Many of us are of the opinion that non-resident tourists should be restricted to the use of recognized campsites on Crown or private land, managed either by the government or by private enterprise. The non-resident should not have the privilege of placing his tent, camper or trailer in any unposted area and using the natural facilities at will, leaving nothing behind except his garbage. Non-resident canoeists should have a prepared route and alternate route designated by the provincial department of natural resources. Non-resident tourists flying in by private or chartered aircraft should have an approved destination. Areas open to use for "fly-in" tourists must be designated and controlled, and only in this way can we prevent the prevalent poaching which is presently going on throughout northwestern Ontario.
Provincial and National parks in Canada, particularly those which are close to the U.S. border, are under very intensive pressure. One of the ways in which we could increase the revenue for park maintenance would be to charge much larger park admission fees for non-residents than is paid by Canadians. This may sound discriminatory but remember that most United States jurisdictions do this, and we are certainly foolish not to follow their example.
Returning to the question of the sale of private land to non-residents, there are some who will argue that there are legal problems associated with measures which would restrict the sale of land to non-residents. The proposition is put forward that the Canadian citizen has the constitutional right to dispose of his property as he sees fit. I submit that this is not the case. Government has the inherent power to act in its social and material interest in laying down conditions respecting aliens. The ownership of our land by large numbers of aliens does have an adverse effect on our social and material well being. The federal and provincial governments not only have the right but also the duty, to enact legislation to deal with this growing and serious problem.
It is interesting to note in the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, reference to these three items: extending and improving the Industrial Development Bank; assistance to credit unions, and aid for small businesses by improving their access to financing facilities. I approve of all these proposals, Mr. Speaker. The Industrial Development Bank has helped entrepreneurs when there was no other place for them to turn. It is true, as the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), has mentioned, that they had to

January 15, 1973

pay a rather high rate of interest to get the money, but at least they have been able to establish or expand their enterprises. There is no question about the fact that it is a matter of urgent concern that we help small businesses with their financing, and everything that we do to assist credit unions will certainly benefit Canada and Canadians. There are now 55,000 credit unions throughout the world with 38 million members. In Canada, every fourth person is a member of a credit union, and 53 million Canadians are enrolled in 4,500 credit unions. Ontario has over one million members in 1,400 credit unions. When the Speech from the Throne speaks of extending and improving the Industrial Development Bank, of improving financing facilities for small businesses, and of assisting credit unions, I certainly agree that these are necessary measures.
The question arises, however, as to what the chartered banks are doing in this country besides paying healthy dividends to their shareholders. Bank stocks are once again among the favourites this year, and no wonder. The combined after-tax profit of eight Canadian chartered banks was $229,956,000 in the year ending October 31, 1972, an increase of 23.2 per cent from the profits in the 1971 fiscal year. Banks are able to maximize their profits by depressing the rates of interest paid on deposits, by raising service charges as much as the market will bear, and by lending only to low risk projects.
It is obvious that projects sponsored by large United States companies will be preferred over ventures by smaller Canadian groups. Mr. Speaker, it is not right that our banks should be helping United States businesses buy out Canadian companies. It seems to me that our banks ought to reflect the national interest in their money lending policies. They ought to invest in Canada in proportion to the resources they derive from Canada. Recent studies have shown that there is no shortage of capital in Canada. New American capital that comes into this country is far exceeded by the export of capital to the United States by Canadians. One of the big failures of our banks is that they do not go far enough in allocating funds to specific regions of Canada, especially developing regions, and in permitting branches there to utilize the money in the best interests of that area.
The Speech from the Throne speaks of measures to increase Canadian participation in the ownership and control of resource projects. There may be some jurisdictional disputes in this regard, Mr. Speaker, but it is clear that action is required if our resource regions are to be truly Canadian rather than merely economic frontiers of the United States.
The rapid increase in the American demand for particular Canadian raw materials arising from the expansion of American industry and the progressive depletion of American domestic sources of supply, has placed Canada in an advantageous, and yet very dangerous position. In the short-term, the effects of this trend are obviously beneficial for Canadian producers, but this in turn leads to a potentially dangerous drain on the total Canadian resources in the long run. A good deal today can become a sell-out tomorrow.
The history of resource development m Canada includes varying degrees of emphasis at different times 25714-19
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
on exploitation, conservation and management. Today, as a basis for resource development and in the making of any new resource policy, the need for orderly management of our resources must be recognized. Although research has not indicated any short-term scarcity, the long-term outlook underlines the need for immediate action to prevent the rapid depletion of our non-renewable resources. Only a policy of orderly management will secure for future generations the optimum benefit from our resources; only a policy of orderly management will be able to rationally bring about a reconciliation of the goals of economic growth and environmental quality.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a brief word about water resources in northwestern Ontario. We have one of the most abundant supplies of fresh water of any region in the world. The government of Canada and the Ontario government are currently engaged in a jointly sponsored study to assess the extent of the water resources in this region. This activity makes us very nervous and just a little uncomfortable, Mr. Speaker. We have had repeated assurances from both the federal and the provincial governments that no massive diversion schemes for our northward flowing rivers are being contemplated. We want very much to believe that, but it is often difficult to trust the word of governments, as the citizens of Manitoba recently discovered with reference to a hydro project in that province. Mr. Speaker, I call on the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) to cease and desist from all studies of our water resources which include the possibility of river diversions. Instead, why not transfer these funds into archeological and ecological research and into economic development projects which will benefit our native people.
I would ask the Minister of the Environment to withdraw, on behalf of the federal government, from this agreement with Ontario, which we believe may be a first step toward another huge hydroelectric project involving damming, flooding and general environmental destruction on a terrifying scale. We in northwestern Ontario do not want something like the James Bay hydro project in Quebec or something like the proposed Churchill River diversion in Manitoba. We respectfully ask both levels of government to recall their engineers and hydrologists-to please get out and stay out. Any attempt to divert our great northward flowing rivers in northwestern Ontario will be met with well organized, lawful resistance. There is now in existence an active citizens group to watch carefully and closely all and any activities related to river diversion in our region. We ask the Minister of the Environment for yet another word of reassurance that diversion schemes are not being contemplated and that any studies of such a possibility will be terminated.

Mr. Speaker, may I join with other hon. members in offering you my congratulations on your election once again as Speaker of this

The Address-Mr. Ritchie
House. I wish Your Honour the very best. I would like also to congratulate the House on its choice of Deputy Speaker. I feel that this choice is a good omen, since I understand that this is the second occasion in Canadian parliamentary history on which the Deputy Speaker has been chosen from the opposition side. This is an important deviation from custom, and we welcome it. In future, perhaps not only the official opposition but other opposition parties might have a representative in that important post.
I also wish to echo the sentiments of the hon. member who spoke just before lunch. I am at one with him in his comments on the CBC, as I come from a riding much the same as his which is served by only one television station. I think the CBC and CRTC have neglected in many ways the primary duty for which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was originally established, the duty of giving service to outlying areas which normally cannot expect to be served by commercial channels. The CBC and CRTC have been far too concerned about the content of programs available to that part of the population which is able to tune in to the American stations, and have forgotten about those portions of the country which can exercise little or no choice in the selection of television programs.
Having said that, may I now turn to the Speech from the Throne. On Monday last, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) launched into his reply to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr.Stanfield). During the course of his discursive and rambling dissertation, he attacked those who had brought his government to a minority position by suggesting that this result was achieved by a misguided group of candidates on my side of the House leading the electorate astray on various subjects, particularly his bilingualism program. Nevertheless, a short study of our recent history will disclose that this is not so.
A review of the past 12 elections will indicate, I suggest, that if the present party system is to continue, we shall be in a minority situation on many occasions to come. In the seven elections since 1957, as opposed to the five before 1957, the Conservative party has had strength in western Canada. In the five elections between 1935 and 1957 the party I support won an average of only eight seats west of Ontario. Since 1957, in seven elections the Conservatives won an average of 42 seats west of the Ontario-Manitoba border. The number of Tory seats in the present parliament is the average that the party has won in the past seven elections. That means that there is a great possibility of increasing Tory strength in western Canada. If present voting trends continue, it is apparent that there will be a good many minority governments.
It gives me great pleasure to note that the vote of Tuesday last found the NDP supporting the Liberal party. We have ample evidence in western Canada to indicate that the NDP is only a wing of the Liberal party, or else how could the minority government of the Pearson regime have withstood the many votes necessary to keep it in power for five years? I welcome this support of the NDP party for the Liberal cause, because it means there has been a polarization that will be good for the politics of Canada. In the last 50 years, western Canada has dissipated its political power in ideological groups supporting

vague causes without any practical possibility of bringing their aims about. Perhaps we are witnessing merely a maturing of political thought in western Canada.
In the past seven elections the decision of western Canadians to give the preponderance of their seats to the Conservative party indicates that they are merely following the lead of Quebec. Quebec in the past 70 years has only deviated on two occasions from supporting the Liberal party. One was in 1958, a period of recent history well known; the other was during the 1920's, when agricultural problems so seriously upset the rural population of Quebec that they voted for a change. This polarization will almost certainly continue and will be a new factor in voting in Canada, particularly western Canada. After all, in our regional country western Canada is in conflict with Quebec on language and culture and with Ontario on economic matters.
The past 100 years of Canadian history show that there has always been a confrontation and compromise between the regions. The main added new factor will be that the compromises will have to take into account the third party, western Canada, and not just Ontario and Quebec. In the book "Pendulum of Power", written by James Beck, Mackenzie King was quoted as saying that during his years as Leader of the Liberal party, in the final analysis he always had to depend on Quebec for his political support.
The Prime Minister suggested that his bilingual program was misunderstood and used by his opponents in a bigoted and unfair way. Mr. Speaker, bilingualism was a factor in western Canada, in my experience at least, but there were many more long standing grievances against the government. Bilingualism was only one of many, many grievances that people expressed. The bilingualism program was an intellectual solution to a very difficult problem. Language is always a divisive force in any nation or group, as often as is religion. In the total population of our country, there are very few bilingual people. To pick out of this small group 25,000 of the 300,000 civil servants who, just because they are bilingual, are to make the executive decisions for this country, will cause intense resentment on the part of those who are unilingual.
It is small wonder the western Canadian voter feels he is largely shut out of the decision making process of the government and that there is little likelihood of any of his representatives attaining a place in this area. It might be said they should accept bilingualism as being necessary for Canadian unity, but I doubt whether most unilingual individuals are willing to accept a second class citizenship because they happen to be unilingual. The farther away from Ottawa these people are, the more unpleasant the policy of bilingualism appears.
The Prime Minister stated there would be some modifications. With a little imagination, the language problem could be solved in a more acceptable manner. If this is to be a two-language country, it is obvious that Canadians must belong to one or the other of these two language groups. The use of the two languages in the civil service will allow both languages to be represented in a way which will correspond to their statistical numbers in the
January 15, 1973

population. This will prevent injustices and imbalances occurring. It would be particularly useful to the minority language group to prevent undue discrimination, an event that could easily happen in the future.
The Prime Minister suggested that many Conservatives and their supporters were not sensitive to the problems of language, particularly as it pertains to Quebec and the separatists. The opposite to sensitivity is allergy. Many people in other parts of Canada are becoming increasingly allergic to this Quebec issue. Perhaps herein lies much of the danger to Canadian unity, probably more so than any other area. It is time to examine other methods of federalism to cope with our linguistic and economic problems.
This government achieved its most abject failure when, with our high rate of unemployment and rapid increase in the labour force, it failed to resolve our trade differences with our neighbour to the south, our largest trading partner. We have always had good relations with the Americans, but in this past 10 years we have seen a diminishing of good will. We all foresee that in the not too distant future there will be restrictions on the easy passage of commerce and people back and forth across the border.
It is difficult to feel that the resolution presented to the House last Friday will not be construed as unilateral censorship of the American bombing of North Viet Nam. We did not register a similar complaint when An Loc and Quangtri, two large cities in South Viet Nam, were razed last fall by Communist artillery. We did not raise any protest whatsoever. We do not know why President Nixon ordered the resumption of bombing, but a captured document indicates that the Viet Cong intended to start a reign of terror as soon as the cease fire came into effect.
There are 14 regular Viet Nam divisions that are ready to give the Viet Cong a helping hand in their task of plunging South Viet Nam into chaos. It seems likely that the president's demand and Hanoi's refusal that these divisions return home was one of the main reasons for the breakdown of the Paris talks. Despite such resolutions by this parliament, Canadians still expect the Americans to have no ill-will and no question of our right to have all possible privileges, and on the most friendly basis, in our relations with the United States. However, it seems unlikely that this sort of behaviour can continue without some reaction.
In a recent situation, Australian seamen imposed a union ban on United States shipping. This was promptly lifted when longshoremen on the U.S. coast refused to unload nine Australian ships carrying meat and wool, even though only two United States ships were involved. Two parties are always involved, and we have to remember this in our dealings with the United States.
The on-again, off-again auto pact talks have been with us for months. This government has made no progress in resolving our trade differences in almost two years. The world is dividing into giant trading blocs, such as the European, the Japanese and the Communist which, surprisingly, is demanding goods and even food from the west. The post-war ideal of free trade is being threatened by these three separate blocs. The other blocs, particularly the European Common Market, seem determined to discriminate against the North American continent. Both
25714-19i
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
Canada and the United States face a world market which is hedged and bedevilled by trade barriers. Within the next two or three years, we will be faced with the protectionist follies of the 1930's.
Canada has her own peculiar problems. We lack a vast domestic market at home and are dependent on the single American market. We are even now affected by high unemployment. How is Canada to maintain its prosperity if the American market is damaged by protectionism? That sentiment is already being exhibited by a frightened congress. As Canada increasingly nourishes manufacturing industries by particular devices of its own, how can it avoid retaliation from the United States? We certainly have an example of this in the Michelin tire case where a United States agency assessed duty on tires because they were built in a plant which was given a DREE grant.
There is also the matter of our natural resources, particularly energy, and how much we will sell to the United States market. There are those who say we should not sell any, but this seems impractical in view of the fact that Canada itself must import energy and other raw materials.
In the past year, Canadian manufacturers have suffered a deterioration in their competitive position because of the appreciation of the Canadian dollar and the introduction of the DISC program. There has been a more fundamental and longer run adverse trend in Canadian manufacturing as far as competitiveness is concerned. The Canada-United States wage differential has narrowed considerably since 1960. All this indicates that the manufacturing industry in Canada, which we have been told so often must provide needed jobs for this decade, is facing a rather bleak future. The cooling of relations with Washington can only mean that our task will be more difficult in the future and Washington will increasingly disregard its counterpart in Ottawa. In the field of relations with Washington, this government has been most derelict.
I now wish to turn to the part of the throne speech that deals with small business. I am very glad this parliament has discovered the small businessman. In the four years that I have been here, this government has not done anything but pass legislation which did not help small businesses in any way. The throne speech indicated that small business has a great place in Canadian life. If this is so, I am sure the small businessman will be one of the first to say he has not had much recognition in the past. The tax structures and the ways of the modern economic system are fast driving him out of existence, yet it is almost the only way in which much of the rural areas of our country can produce and provide a living for their people. In the past four years, this government has shown little or no awareness of the small business, the small businessman and the small entrepreneur.
When speaking about small business, we must also consider agriculture which is almost wholly carried on in the small business context. It is still the basic industry of Canada. It is significant that even with the rise of food prices, the next cash income of farmers in 1972 will be less than in the previous year, 1971. I think the same will hold true for most other small businesses. The problem of small business in the past few years has been its inability to adjust to rising costs and wages, both of which have

January 15, 1973
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
been rising considerably faster than the ability of small business to cope. By the time it has been able to adjust either by raising prices or increasing productivity, wages and costs have moved on to a new plateau. In the case of the farming industry, the unit prices have not changed appreciably in 20 years. Farmers have had to adjust by increased productivity and, at the same time we have seen an exodus of people from the farm working force to other industry. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) suggested to us what a great thing it is that the corporation tax on small manufacturing businesses is to be lowered from 25 per cent to 20 per cent. But it was 20 per cent under the old tax law, and it will be appreciated that very few small businesses will fall into the manufacturing and processing category.
Recent tax changes dealt a heavy blow to small business. In agriculture, the loss of the basic herd, straightline depreciation on machinery and capital gains tax are especially onerous. The tax changes in the recent act affecting small corporations such as the wiping out of the low tax rate on investment income will prevent the accumulation of money in the corporation for expansion. Small corporations must save money for a period of time before expanding.
The small business entrepreneur starting out finds himself in formidable difficulties. As well as attempting to compete, and build his business, he must hire a tax accountant to keep him out of trouble with National Revenue, otherwise, through some tax misfortune, he may face severe penalties and the possible loss of what he has accumulated. He also must comply with numerous regulations, laws and special requirements in order to meet various standards. All this detracts from his ability to manage his business. But the government will remedy this, they say, because they will provide consultants. Mr. Speaker, I do not think any small businessman will be thanking the government for sending men around to tell him how to run his business better.
It is difficult for small businessmen to procure the necessary capital, and I doubt if the Industrial Development Bank will be particularly helpful. It is generally considered by many small business people that if the government has to finance them, it is hardly worth being in business. There is a great reluctance on the part of most small business entrepreneurs to rely on government loans and government handouts. The problem of financing for the small businessman is that the pools of capital normally available in the past have dried up or else are out of his reach. The introduction of the pension plan and registered retirement plans has meant that, at least in small communities, most capital is siphoned off to the large cities and it is not practical to invest it in the place it came from.
Pension plans are now the largest investment factor in the market at the present time. The government's interest in small business is laudable, but one has to face the fact that the individual entrepreneur is not faring very well in the present day business world. Generally, those who would be successful small business people can command a good salary in the wage structure of the commercial world. In the early years of his life and of his family, this

is a very important consideration. In later years, the prospect of capital gains and estate tax at the end of his career, makes being a small business entrepreneur not particularly attractive. The government will have to do much more than to advise small business or to attempt to bbrrow it into existence before there will be significant improvement in the small business position.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word about inflation. At this time, with the rapid rise in prices, I would advise that we look at all our options to achieve price stability. New policy options should be introduced to achieve a faster rate of real growth and lower unemployment rates and yet establish a climate of price stability so necessary for the future. There should be a reduction in all federal sales and excise taxes. This would exert downward pressure on the price levels because it would be passed on to the customer; a sales tax cut has an expansionary effect on real consumer demands as it lowers prices. Incidence of sales tax bears most heavily on the lower income group, so sales tax cuts are the best means of distributing purchasing power to those with low incomes; they are far more effective than an income tax cut.
Those with fixed incomes, the unemployed and those who have borne the brunt of the anti-inflationary program, would benefit more from sales tax cuts than from income tax reductions. The impact of the decline in prices would be more significant than a cut in income tax. A sales tax cut would reduce government revenues, but economic expansion would be stimulated and part of the tax revenue loss would be recovered. A sales tax cut increases real income, reduces wage demands and has the most deflationary effect of any tax cut. It would have the added advantage of helping the lowest income group more than an income tax cut would. Of course, many other things ought to be done in conjunction with a policy to contain inflation.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne was full of vague generalities. It can be interpreted to mean almost anything. We shall have to wait for specific legislation to be brought down before we can make any reasonable assessment of what the speech really means.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the encomiums which have been heaped on the heads of the presiding officers since this debate began have been fulsome indeed, and at this stage the repetition of those words of praise, even though sincere, might be somewhat ritualistic. Nevertheless, this debate does give us an opportunity to pay our respects to the president officers and to proclaim our devotion to the institution of the Speakership in the Canadian House of Commons.
Today, the speakership is a strong, vital and valuable institution. Without it, the House of Commons could not operate. The standing of the Speakership at the moment is due in part to the qualities of those who now hold the office and of those who have held the office in the past. It also derives in part from the standing which the Speaker enjoys arising from the fact that he is an elected member of the House; he comes to this House through the same process of election as all other hon. members. It has been suggested from time to time that an institution be created
January 15, 1973

called a permanent Speakership, something which would involve the creation of a special House of Commons seat.
The Speaker would thus be relieved of the necessity of seeking election in an ordinary constituency. For my part, if any such innovation involved a device which eliminated the necessity for a Speaker or a potential Speaker running for election like other commoners, then I would be entirely opposed to it. In this view I am supported by opinions of two former Prime Ministers, the late Mr. Pearson, and of the present right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). Mr. Pearson, speaking in a debate in this House in 1965, and referring to the possibility I have mentioned, stated:
This device would certainly transform the Speaker from being an equal with his fellow members over whose deliberations he presides, into-and I say this in no derogatory sense-some type of parliamentary functionary, and I suggest that the change might even reduce the prestige of your office.
Later in the same debate, in fact the following day, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said:
I do not believe in the principle that a constituency should be set up for the purpose of providing a Speaker. He would then cease to be the first commoner that he is because he would be there by choice and not election.
I believe the very fact that so many hon. members have paid sincere tributes to the presiding officers indicates that at the present time the Canadian Speakership is working very well indeed, and any changes probably would be in the wrong direction.
Mr. Speaker, you do make a very imposing figure in the Chair. Your physical presence is very imposing, and no less imposing is your fair mindedness, your studiousness and your friendliness. I congratulate you as the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) for having become the Deputy Speaker of this House of Commons. Your selection as Deputy Speaker from the ranks of the official opposition underlines the simple reality that if this House of minorities is to produce and deliver for the people of Canada it will require the co-operation of all the parties in the House of Commons, and that reality will exist whether this party or the party opposite happens to sit in the treasury benches.
The mover and seconder of the address in reply performed exceedingly well, despite the fact that they were competing for attention in an atmosphere of concern and tension in respect of the fate of the twenty-ninth parliament. Other new members on all sides of the House made impressive contributions to the debate and I congratulate them most warmly, as I do congratulate them on their election to the House of Commons.
May I refer in particular to the maiden speech of the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) who pleased us all with her historical perception in a well delivered speech. She comes to the House of Commons well endowed. She is a Cape Bretoner and a MacDonald. As she pointed out, the first member for Kingston was a Macdonald, a Conservative like herself. In the intervening years, the Macdonald presence was further felt in Kingston by the representation of that historic city in the House of Commons by the late Angus L. Mac-
The Address-Mr. MacEachen
donald, a former Premier of Nova Scotia who, when he served Kingston, was the Minister of Naval Services in the Mackenzie King administration.
Of course, he succeeded the late Norman McLeod Rogers who represented Kingston, another distinguished Nova Scotian who met his untimely death in the service of his country. The late Angus L. was a great political figure in his day and a friend of a number of us presently in the House of Commons. He was certainly a friend and political competitor of the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). He had just about everything. He was a Cape Bretoner, a Macdonald and a Liberal.
The hon. member for Kingston and The Islands bears the name of a Scottish heroine whose memory still lives because of her bravery in several historic episodes, but especially for her ingenuity in planning the escape from the English searchers of Prince Charles Edward Stuart known in history as "Bonnie Prince Charlie". Dr. Johnson, and I am not referring to Dr. James Johnson, who will be well known to the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands, but Dr. Samuel Johnson wrote about the original Flora during his tour of the Hebrides in 1772 saying that "Flora MacDonald is a name that will be mentioned in history, and if courage and self-sacrifice be virtues, mentioned with honour." Of course, his prediction was fulfilled for, if you travel in Scotland today, you will find memorials in Inverness, Skye and Uist, dedicated to the original Flora MacDonald.
May I make a prediction today, Mr. Speaker, a la Samuel Johnson. My prediction is that the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands, the modern, perceptive Flora MacDonald, will bring in our day added lustre to the old name and the old clan, and will deserve a secure place in our political history, though I hasten to add that I doubt whether such an outcome will excite the enthusiasm of the right hon. member for Prince Albert.
Is this a proposal?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I now turn to a less agreeable subject, namely the current parliamentary situation. I suppose parliamentary maturity, like personal maturity, is to accept what comes of an election and to make the best of circumstances as we find them. Certainly no member of the House of Commons wished that the election results would be just what they are. In fact, the results were not wished upon us by ourselves, they were imposed upon us by the will of the Canadian people. Our job, inconvenient as it may be for some or all of us, is to accept the situation and to work within it as well as we can.
The NDP, the Social Credit party and the government itself have all fully accepted the results of the election and have declared their intention of doing their best to work within this parliament in order that parliament itself can work on behalf of the people of Canada. The government has accepted its responsibility of presenting a legislative program and the NDP and the Social Credit party have accepted the responsibility of examining that program and accepting or rejecting it on its merits. Absent from this acceptance of the present situation is the official opposition.

January 15, 1973
The Address-Mr. MacEachen
I have examined the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Peace River and the right hon. member for Prince Albert and nowhere do I find any indication that either of those hon. gentlemen is ready to accept the results of the election, let alone decide to work constructively within this House for the welfare of the people of Canada. They who accused this government of arrogance on every possible occasion have shown the greatest possible arrogance themselves by saying the results of the election are not for them and the twenty-ninth parliament is not their bag at all. The result is, of course, displeasing to them. They have made no commitment to make parliament work. They have no desire to prolong the life of this parliament. In my opinion, they have no desire, even if they did form a government, to place a legislative program before the House of Commons. The plan of the official opposition is absolutely clear from their conduct, and from their speeches since the session began.
Your plan is quite clear.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Their plan was to propose, as they did, a non-confidence motion against the government, in the fervent expectation that that motion would be accepted and the government would fall. But having put the nonconfidence motion before the House, they then hesitated before the full effect of that motion could be dealt with, and proposed a motion that the House adjourn.
No, no-the debate.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That ham-handed effort-Mr. Speaker, I thank the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). The motion was that the debate adjourn. That was certainly a departure from the plan. We took the attitude that the first duty of the government was not to present a legislative program but to secure and test the confidence of the House. That was the attitude taken by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he faced a minority House in October, 1957.
At that time the then Leader of the Opposition refused to put a non-confidence motion. The then Prime Minister, now the right hon. member for Prince Albert, was so upset because it transgressed parliamentary propriety and might deny him the opportunity of seeking the confidence of the House, that he complained. Indeed, he complained in a number of ways. As a matter of fact, I find his comments on that day quite useful.
You will find them useful on a lot of other days, too.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Now, he has a changed attitude. At that time, speaking about Mr. St. Laurent, who was the Leader of the Opposition, he said, as recorded at page 48 of Hansard for October 16,1957:
I could not quite follow him in the attitude that he took all the way through his speech. It was an attitude of criticism-sometimes captious criticism-this was wrong, that was wrong-
Can you imagine how the right hon. gentleman has changed, from the moment that he found criticism was

wrong, until the speech that he made in the House the other day?
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
However, he went on to say, and this is the point I want to draw to the attention of hon. members opposite:
If everything that is being presented is wrong or subject to criticism, why not do that which under ordinary circumstances would be the proper attitude to adopt?
