Why not permit a vote to take place regarding that matter which above all others is of the first consideration, whether or not we do enjoy the confidence of the House of Commons?
That sound principle, like many of the policies which the right hon. gentleman advocated, has been abandoned by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). He sought to interrupt a debate on a non-confidence motion and asked the government to present legislation- a government in which he had no confidence. What parliamentary folly is that!
So frustrated were hon. members opposite when the House seized the opportunity to defeat the official opposition, that some of them interpreted that procedural vote as a vote against old age pensions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: So it was.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What frustration!
Shame!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: One of them said, referring to the government, "They stood in opposition to immediate relief for the old people of Canada". Another hon. member said, "They are voting against the consideration of old age pensions at this time." What a strange interpretation to be made in that frenzy of disappointment. Of course, what drove them up the wall was that the House itself refused to co-operate with them in their objective of bringing this parliament to a quick end, because that was their purpose, to bring down the government, to move over here, and then dissolve and have a quick election.
No.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no sense to their speeches. The Leader of the Opposition made a long speech. He did not say, "We must make this parliament work". He did not say, "I have a program." He did not turn to the Social Credit or to the NDP and say, "Members of this House, I have a better program than the Speech from the Throne."
That was obvious in the election itself.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
All he said was, "They stole my program. It's stolen goods. It's grand larceny". This government, Mr. Speaker, is in the wonderful position, the enviable position, of being accused by both the NDP and the Conservative party of having expropriated their programs. The only difference is that the NDP is honest enough to give the House an opportunity to deal with its expropriated program, while the official opposition has no alternative to offer. Up to the moment, it is asking for the confidence of all hon. members but it has not told us what program it wishes to bring forward.
January 15, 1973

The official opposition did not tell us its pension program. It only wanted to stop the House, stop the clock, stop parliament and deal with pensions. But, I repeat, no speaker in the ranks of the official opposition has yet stated what their position is on old age pensions. Where do they stand? Is it the position that the Leader of the Opposition took during the election campaign, or is it a new position? What is their program if it is better than the expropriated program in the Speech from the Throne? The House did not co-operate. Why should it co-operate with the political ambitions of the Conservative party to form a government, dissolve parliament, and hold a midwinter election without putting any program before the House?
Shame.
That's hocus-pocus.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peace River has said in his speech, "Let us not listen to government proposals. Let us not find out what they have in mind. We know all about them because they have been in the government for a number of years." Mr. Speaker, in case any of the members of the Social Credit or the NDP are tempted to place the official opposition over here may I refer to a number of their accomplishments and achievements in the past.
Take the question of unemployment, now before the House in the form of a non-confidence motion moved by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) who, in his statesmanlike appeal for support for his party, called the NDP fakers and charlatans. Are those the words of a party that wants the House of Commons to work, that wants to prolong the life of parliament?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Was he that moderate?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Today we are being asked by the hon. member for South Shore to deny confidence to the government because of its bad record on unemployment. We all know the facts about the present unemployment figures, and there really is not much consolation in telling the House that the performance of the government in the field of unemployment is much better than the performance of the last Conservative government under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You have the highest record of unemployment today.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The highest point of unemployment came in January, 1961. The highest absolute number of unemployed occurred in that month when it reached 690,000.
That was five elections ago.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, five elections ago, and now the same crowd of people are asking to become the government of this country.

Oh, oh.
The Address-Mr. MacEachen

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There were 690,000 unemployed persons at that time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: How about 1896?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I know my hon. friend has rejected the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), but I did not expect him to do it openly in the House of Commons. That number of unemployed, 690,000, was the highest in this country. It has never been reached under the administration of this government. Last month the figures were high enough at 584,000, but in the meantime the Canadian labour force has grown from six and a half million to almost nine million.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: How was inflation then, and what was the cost of living?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Our performance, on any comparison, is distinctly better than anything that could be offered by that group of persons opposite if they formed a government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Why don't you say "nobodies"?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the Leader of the Opposition formed the government, he would have about the same group of men around him, the same administrators. The former and potential minister of trade and commerce is right in front of us in potentia, and so is the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) who was associated with the former government. They might say that the Leader of the Opposition is new, that he was not part of that crowd. He was an acquiescent and quiescent supporter of the former right hon. gentleman in those years when unemployment in the Atlantic provinces ran consistently higher than it has done this year or in any year of Liberal administration. He did everything in the election of 1963 to put his "friend of high unemployment" back in office as the prime minister of Canada. Perhaps we have new blood in the person of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) and new blood in the person of the hon. member for Saint Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner)-these recycled Grits who have now come to sit on the Conservative benches. I would suggest that if this House wants Liberalism it would prefer it in a pure rather than a corrupted form.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The old group has the stench of decay.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They weep about pensions. It is hard to believe but when this crowd was in office the last time they left the old age security benefit at $65. They had been six years in office.
Tell us about six buck Harris.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That goes back seven elections.
Tell us all about the six buck boys.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
They left the old age pension at $65, in April of 1973 the maximum GIS will be $156.75. Compare that performance, allowing the pensions to remain at such

January 15, 1973
The Address-Mr. MacEachen
a low level, with the performance of the Liberal government under the former prime minister and under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The House of Commons is asked to vote for that crown and to put them in office in the light of that performance and in the light of their failure to tell us what they propose to do.
Tell us when six buck Harris raised it to $46.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sorry that the right hon. member for Prince Albert is not in his seat.
You should be glad that he is not.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is familiar with those years about which I have been speaking because it was in those years that he became so familiar with the practice of bundling about which he showed such a complete grasp in his notable discourse last week. In the 1962-63 parliament we were all here and we watched the great bundling that occurred between the right hon. gentleman and the Social Credit group in the House of Commons. That was an honourable course, so the prime minister of the day told us. It was honourable to prolong the life of parliament, and in order to prolong it he sought and received the support of the Social Credit party.
He did not seek it and he did not receive it, and you know it. Tell the truth, Allan. It is a poor speech but at least tell the truth.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Social Credit party prolonged the life of that government in every vote except on motions it moved itself, and it did so consistently until February 4, 1963.
Tell us about the time when you supported funny money.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was on that fateful day-
Do you remember that day? That was a fine, honourable vote, was it not?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the minister but the time allotted to him has expired. It can be extended with unanimous consent.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, according to our previous practice the minister would be allowed another five or ten minutes to finish his remarks, and that would be agreeable at this time, but we would not want this to go on all day long.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has been given extended time.
Give us five more minutes on six buck Harris and the funny money vote. You were so proud of them in those days.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I must say I have not been receiving very much co-operation from the opposition in making this address, but I did think it was important to mention that history just did not begin with the opening of the

twenty-ninth parliament, that we have had a minority situation before. We had a minority situation in 1962 and 1963. The government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert survived with the support of the Social Credit group until February 4, 1963 when between six and eight o'clock, the then leader of the Social Credit party changed his mind. What happened? I will tell you what happened.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert let him fall out of bed between six and eight o'clock that night and he changed his vote. Before six o'clock he said, "An election in Canada precipitated at this time by the events of the last three days and carrying an anti-American overtone would be a tragedy for Canada". That was before six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. After eight o'clock he moved a subamendment.
That was before you got to him.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That brought down the government of the day and, mind you-
What is all this proving?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is proving a number of things.
Just give me one. Come on, let's have one thing that this is proving. You know it is not proving anything except that you are on cloud nine.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it simply proves that what was then honourable in the mind of the right hon. member for Prince Albert today is ignoble because he is not the beneficiary of the support of members of the House that kept him in office in those days. It is instructive in another way-
Watch your voice, Allan; you are getting excited. Don't let your voice break like that. Think of your health.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is instructive in another way, Mr. Speaker, because the other day the right hon. member for Prince Albert talked about "monstrous constitutional doctrines".
They have been modified over the week-end.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
He is obviously drawing a lot on his own career. He was defeated on that night of February 5. He had called parliament the preceding September but did not sit all those days because there was a fairly long adjournment and his government fell on February 5. He had been sustained on about eight substantive motions that involved confidence but as I recollect, he did not, when he lost, resign. He did not say, "I am through"; he went to Government House and got a dissolution. When the then Leader of the New Democratic Party spoke that night he ended by saying, "Let the people decide"; the then leader of the Social Credit party said, "Let the people decide" and the right hon. gentleman got his dissolution and went to the people.
January 15, 1973

The thought that any Prime Minister today would contemplate the possibility of dissolution sends the right hon. gentleman almost into hysterics.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You would not say that if he were here.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they have talked about Sir John A. Macdonald. We heard in the dulcet tones of the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) that he was the father of our country and the father of the Conservative party. We know what happened from 1867 to 1873, or whatever the dates are. Sir John A. Macdonald lost nine votes in this House-he lost them on supply, he lost them on money bills, he lost them on important government legislation, including a tariff measure; he lost them on all these things but he did not resign. When it is suggested that the present government might accept a defeat and not resign it is called a "monstrous doctrine". That is the theology of the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert.
I remember reading at one time-
Are you going even farther back?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. I am not. I remember reading at one time-
King Charles lost his head.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the interruptions of the hon. gentleman are becoming offensive.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would like him to please refrain from further interruptions while I am making this speech.
Hear, hear!
If you can't stand the heat, you had better get out of the kitchen.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not the heat I am worried about it is the lack of light coming from the other side.
I remember reading a biography of Sir John A. Macdonald, the father of our country, in which it was stated that at one of his meetings a supporter, overcome with emotion, got up and said to him, "Sir John, you will never die". Mr. Speaker, he may still live in this House of Commons. As we quote some of these precedents created by the father of our country, as we find our way through this difficult minority government, we will not hesitate to lean on those precedents in order to meet situations as we find them.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is nothing dishonourable or monstrous about that.
Allan, have you seen a doctor lately?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noted the words of the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis). He said, "Our votes are available only upon delivery"; he said, "We
The Address-Mr. MacEachen
take a COD policy". I interpret that to mean "confidence on delivery". In this world in which we live, I am prepared to accept the brutal consequences of that brutal statement.
In the Speech from the Throne we have put before the House a series of proposals that up to the present have enjoyed the confidence of the House. We intend to deliver on these proposals.
You had better. We will kick you out of bed if you don't.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We intend to deliver and bring forward our legislative program in a way that will continue to justify the confidence of a majority of members of this House of Commons. But remember this: we in this party represent a historic party. We have integrity, we have identity, and in seeking our way through this minority House we do not intend to deform the integrity or identity of our party position, nor do we expect any other party to deform its integrity or its identity. We will work through this House of Commons week by week, and day by day to introduce a legislative program.
I want to say especially to members of the Social Credit party and the New Democratic Party that we cannot be expected to waive the normal procedures of parliament and the normal procedures of government merely to stay in office. We will bring in a budget when it is possible and when it is normal. We cannot bring it in tomorrow or an hour before a demanded time simply because there is an atmosphere of tension and uncertainty in the House. We cannot do impossible things, but one of our major commitments to the House was that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in his budget would bring forward major new fiscal and other measures to deal responsively and effectively with our most pressing economic and social problems.
Bully for you!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That budget will be brought forward and the House will have an opportunity, in due course, to deal with it and to decide whether it has the confidence of a majority of members. We have committed ourselves to bringing in new programs in the field of small business- alleged to be stolen goods! We have committed ourselves through managerial assistance and through amendments to the industrial development bank to assist with new programs for the business community. We have indicated our intention of bringing in an improved foreign takeovers bill and we have indicated our intention, through the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), to consider major directions in consultation with the provinces in our social security system. The minister has already committed himself to a substantial increase in old age pensions.
The Minister for Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) has indicated to the House that those programs will be changed and remodelled in certain ways in order to bring about the decentralization of decision-making and to improve co-ordination. The minister responsible for urban affairs and housing has brought before the House a very ambitious new program involving hundreds of millions of dollars. It projects changes to the National
294

January 15, 1973
The Address-Mr. Gleave
Housing Act that will provide more help for Canadians to buy houses.
Hon. members opposite are asking, "What is your legislative priority?" I have asked the opposition House leaders to make suggestions. We will bring forward a program just as quickly as we can complete the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, which will be concluded tomorrow night hopefully, or Wednesday night. Then we will proceed with items on the order paper. We will try to deal responsibly with the conflicting demands on the time of the House. We shall deal with economic issues and other matters, including supply, which must be dealt with by the House. At least, the House must be given an opportunity to deal with that question. Then, there is the all-important issue of capital punishment. We will balance all this and present a program to the House. The government has declared its intention in the Speech from the Throne, and in speeches made by ministers, that it is prepared to produce a program to put before the House and to accept the consequences of a minority situation. We intend to live up to our side of the commitment. In this case, the government will pose and the House will dispose. Those are the rules of the game that I fully and enthusiastically accept and under which I wish to work.

Mr. Speaker, may I, as previous hon. members have done, express my appreciation of your election as Speaker of the House and say how glad I am to see Your Honour once again undertaking former duties. In my speech this afternoon I want to talk to some extent about farmers and agriculture. First, I want to make a few general comments about the Speech from the Throne which is, I suppose one might say, a declaration of intent on the part of the government. The government has laid out its view of the Canadian economy and of the situation of the Canadian people at this time. The throne speech refers to the needs of the Canadian people and of those things that need to be corrected. It covers much ground and much of that cannot be dealt with at once. I suppose, as is often the case in the affairs of man, we will need patience in the matter. I think that many in Canada may not have as much patience as some of us here have.
Let me note some of those items that are mentioned in the Speech. There is access to foreign markets. Grain exports are expected to grow. There is a commitment to job expansion. Capital works projects are mentioned. It is about time they were recognized. According to the throne speech special attention will be given to the four western provinces. There is a reference to a meeting to be held between the governments of those provinces and the federal government. That will be good for the medium and long term. There is also a proposal, already before the House, to examine food prices and how those prices are affecting the Canadian people. We are told that those prices have increased by 5 per cent in the past year. The one thing I want to do, Mr. Speaker, is keep a few things in perspective.
The other day the oil companies, that is those which refine our fuel, in concert announced a 2 cent per gallon

increase in the price of diesel fuel. That represents an 8 per cent increase in one of the most important inputs affecting the operation of the grain farmer of western Canada and of the other farmers across Canada. I noticed that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) showed a good deal of equanimity when he was questioned in the House the other day on this subject. He did not seem to be bothered because this extra charge was to be visited on the food producers and, indeed, the general public of this country. It was no great concern of his.
I was first elected to this House in 1968. Between 1968 and 1972, Gulf Oil discontinued its refinery operations in Saskatoon. Imperial Oil is now about ready to completely discontinue the operation of its refinery in Regina. Perhaps that move has already been completed. Mr. Speaker, as a Member of Parliament representing Saskatoon, I protested against the discontinuance of the refinery operation there, partly because that action would take away from Saskatoon many relatively well paying jobs, because after all the petroleum industry is one of the better paying industries, and partly because that industry was developed in Saskatoon without any DREE grants, special assistance or anything like that. Like the co-operative refinery in Regina, it grew and developed by raising its own capital. When I and some officials in Saskatoon inquired why the Imperial oil operation was being discontinued, the answer we were given was that the move would result in greater efficiency. In so many words, the answer we were given was "Never mind, you small town boys; you do not know what this is all about. We will close down this operation and create a big refinery somewhere else, and the result will be greater efficiency." What is the result of that efficiency now, Mr. Speaker? The result is another 2 cents per gallon on the price of diesel fuel. That increase, as I said before, the minister responsible viewed with a good deal of equanimity. Let me tell him that the people in Saskatchewan do not view it with equanimity. There are people in Saskatchewan now who are saying that if the oil industry of Canada cannot do better than that, we had better nationalize it.
Hear, hear!

You do not have to be an out and out socialist to find that the performance of the oil companies is entirely unacceptable. You need not be anything but an ordinary farmer who is getting doggone tired of being gouged. That is all. So, Mr. Speaker, I do not think you need look too far to fathom the reason for the shortage of fuel oil in the United States. Those in responsible positions have decided it is more important to bomb North Viet Nam than to heat the United States.
Hear, hear!

We in this country should not have to pay extra money for fuel oil for that reason. The people of the United States can decide their priorities. They are a sovereign nation as are we. They decide their priorities and we should decide our priorities. Our priorities should be an efficient refining system which passes on some of the benefits of increased productivity and increased efficien-
January 15, 1973

cy to the consumers of this country. The farmers are a large part of the consuming public.
The fertilizer manufacturers have announced that they intend to get their pound of flesh shortly. In an article in the Globe and Mail, there is a report by Mr. R. R. Baxter informing the United Co-operatives of Ontario that there will not be sufficient fertilizer next spring. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) knows of the United Co-operatives of Ontario. If there is any other message in that article except that the price of fertilizer will be increased, I would like to know it. The signals are out. The notice is being given.
The price of fertilizer was also increased last spring. I received correspondence from farmers at that time. I asked the then Minister of Agriculture if some action could be taken to deal with this increase in price and whether there was sone kind of combine or a monopoly administering prices. The answer I received was "No, there is nobody in this chicken-house except us chickens. There is nothing wrong here, boys. There is no combine and nobody is getting together to set prices. Everything is open and above board." I expect that the same reply will be given this time if anyone should ask. Anyone who expects the price of food to go down at a time when the oil companies are increasing the price of fuel to the farmer and the fertilizer companies are getting ready to increase their prices is just whistling "Dixie". You can bet your life the farm machinery companies will not be far behind.
They are away out in front.

They are probably away out in front. I am pleased that the federal government will be getting together with the governments of the western provinces to determine what can be done in western Canada. I would be even more pleased if the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) could tell us in the very near future what they intend to do about these immediate problems. I would be pleased also if the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) could tell us what the government intends doing about a decent transportation system. He does not have to wait until the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) meets with the western provinces. All he has to do is talk to Mr. Benson, the man the government put in charge of the Canadian Transport Commission a short while ago. A better idea yet would be to pick up the phone, fire him, and put someone else in that position.
Hear, hear!

We in the grain business know that our ability to export is limited by the kind of transport made available to move grain. I referred to the article which mentioned the increase in the price of fertilizer. The limiting factor on the fertilizer companies' ability to supply will depend on their ability to receive shipments of potash and make shipments of fertilizer. We in this country are very dependent on transportation. We realize that our transportation facilities are not adequate to meet the needs of this country.
If there is one thing Canadians know how to do, it is to build railroads and rolling stock. We build and sell locomotives. Apparently no one in power is willing to tell
The Address-Mr. Gleave
the CNR and CPR to provide their services to the people who require them. It is about time somebody did this.
Hear, hear!

I received a letter from the Canadian Telecommunications Union. They complained that approximately 200 of their number were being laid off. They also noted that Saturday service in the city of Prince Albert will be cut. Apparently we can no longer afford to have telegraphic service on Saturdays in a city the size of Prince Albert. The government fouled up the Saturday delivery of mail, and now the railroads are fouling up Saturday service by the telegraphic system. In the same letter, it was pointed out that two jobs would be lost in the Saskatoon office. In due time there will probably be days when the offices in Saskatoon will be closed. What is the matter with Canadians that we permit this kind of nonsense. It is about time we became more realistic about looking at the needs of agriculture. I have referred to the cost side and also the fact that we need a more adequate transportation system.
It is stated in the throne speech that the government is going to set up an equitable pricing system for grain and livestock. I do not know what genius is at work on that. The government also says there will be an efficient and timely movement of grain. I am in favour of that. It is also stated in the throne speech, and I quote:
The Government supports the principle of an equitable relationship of prices of feed grain to livestock feeders in various areas of Canada.
I suppose the government intends to take some action, but I want to make myself perfectly clear. As far as I am concerned, the Canadian Wheat Board is the bargaining agent for the western farmer for wheat, oats and barley. Anyone or any government that proposes to take away that bargaining power or interfere with the right of the Canadian Wheat Board to price those commodities as it sees fit in its day-to-day judgment will receive the undivided opposition of members in this party who represent farm areas. When I see the gobbledygook in that statement, I am rather suspicious. I would prefer to have the objectives set out in plain and simple language such as an ordinary farmer can understand.
We are not carried away by the present grain situation. At the present time, worldwide, we find a situation which one would have to go back a long while in history to match. We are at a period when drought has caused crop failure in Russia, next to China the largest wheat producer in the world, also in India and in Australia, which are the other major producers in addition to Canada and the United States. At the same time that drought has been experienced in Indonesia in the rice area, floods occurred in the Philippines. A world wide shortage of grain arises automatically from such a situation. There Is, besides, pressure on other foodstuffs-oilseeds and proteins generally.
The biggest stress will always be on transportation. The farmer is a realist. He does not expect the present situation to last forever, anymore than he expected the situation where large amounts were in storage in the late
296

January 15, 1973
The Address-Mr. Gleave
sixties to last forever. About the only true thing one learns about the grain industry worldwide is that is is unpredictable.
Those who observe it for any length of time know they have to swing with the changes in productivity and demand. So, what we need is a policy which will meet such a situation. This hinges on transportation and storage just as much as on production. We hope that in the present session of parliament the government will come forward with a storage policy comprehensive enough that the farmer may look forward with confidence to adequate service in this field and in transportation. These are the areas in which we have suffered, mainly.
The government has also promised to take a look at storage policy in western Canada. If they were to rely to some extent on the advice given them by those who build and operate the co-operative systems they might be able to come up with a rational plan for change in the system without wrecking it in the process. I get scared when I hear some experts talking about collecting the grain in 80 elevators, trucking it into the terminals and then hauling it out again by rail.
Better not try it.
We must be concerned about preserving a viable farm industry. I do not think any nation has been better served than Canada when it comes to food production, in terms of both supply and price.
Quality, too.

The days of cheap land are over. We have occupied it all. The days of cheap labour for the farmer are over, and this House, as well as all those responsible for policy making, had better recognize that fact. The most valuable part of the farm scene at this time, next to the land itself, are the people who know how to operate a farm and how to use the land. And there are not too many of them. There are not enough. The small farm development legislation which the government devised last session is not properly designed to meet the needs of land transfer in this country. It is designed to enlarge farms, and within its limits, those who have managerial ability and who can gather together sufficient capital will be able to take advantage of it. But the real problem for farmers is in the area of labour, the cost of land and the cost of money. There is only one province which is trying to devise a means of transfer which will not keep the farm population permanently in hock, and that is Saskatchewan. I say this even though Saskatchewan is my own province. But the federal government has up to this point refused to co-operate with the province in implementing that scheme.
Shame.

They are willing to sign up as far as their own plan is concerned, but not with the Saskatchewan one. Yet this is an area which, if it is not dealt with today, will have to be met next year or the year after.
I wanted to put some of these views before the House this afternoon. There are other questions, too, which will have to be dealt with. We are trying, as a country, to feel

our way through, for example, a new marketing plan for the marketing of poultry. We are striking out on somewhat new lines, finding new ways of doing things. And I suppose we will encounter certain pitfalls. But the only man I know who never succeeded in doing anything wrong was the man who never tried anything. As long as nothing new happens to him he is alright, but if anything new happens he is in serious trouble.
Finally, there is the whole question of transportation. I plead with all those who are responsible to take a fresh look at the proposals to abandon branch lines on the wholesale scale now proposed. I have looked at some of the plans-for example the one involving Rosthern at the north end of my constituency, the line from Langham to Laird and Carlton, and so on. If we let the railways take up the rails then we are looking at a different rail system from the one we have now. The thinking of the MacPher-son Commission is out of date. I suggest it is hopelessly out of date. This commission sat for some time and then said to the people of Canada: "If you want to get the answer to the railways system, rely on competition". In western Canada competition between railways does not really exist. If it did exist in a pure economic sense, one or the other of the two railroads would be broke. This is a basic theory of competition. If competition goes on long enough the weakest competitor will be pushed to the wall. One system would go broke and the other would run the total rail system. This has not happened because full competition does not exist. The ideas of the MacPherson commission are out of date and they should be discarded.
What we should be looking at today is the use of energy. We are being told the amount of energy is limited. Energy, if it is wasted, will certainly run out but it is limited even if it is used properly. I am sure that if someone studied this whole question of transporting grain, he would find that in terms of energy the cheapest way to get grain out of these areas where branch lines exist is by rail. You need one locomotive and a string of boxcars, and this would require the least energy. If we disregard the desire of the CPR for profit, it can be established that this method of transportation is the cheapest per ton mile. If we are foolish enough to allow the railway companies to tear up lines, and we then build roads and buy trucks I suggest we are losing our marbles. If you want to help the people of western Canada I suggest that this whole matter be placed on the agenda for consideration at the meeting with the western provinces. These are the things we are concerned about in the west.
We could go on and refer to things like pollution. I suggest we would have less pollution if we hauled this grain by rail rather than by truck. The suggestion in the throne speech in respect of the government picking up half the cost of crop insurance is a good one. Up to now crop insurance has not been able to cope with disasters in areas such as the Peace River which is suffering a severe crop loss at this moment. Crop insurance has not been able to cope with such disasters because, in large areas of the country, the farmers have not bought it. One might ask why they have not bought it. The answer is that it did not pay enough in relation to the cost and they could not afford the premiums.
January 15, 1973

If there is to be an insurance scheme which will meet the needs of those involved in disasters, and they are bound to occur across the country, this is a start in the right direction. I do not know whether the new proposals will be adequate. I suppose we would have to obtain actuarial figures before we would know. Because of the nature of the climate in Canada, whether you are growing potatoes in Prince Edward Island or wheat in Saskatchewan, insurance has to be such that it can compensate for losses in times of major disasters. I suppose the only area in Canada which is not subject to these difficulties to a large degree is the area of southern or southwestern Ontario. The people in those areas enjoy the best climate and growing season in Canada. If this measure meets the requirements for an adequate crop insurance program, we will have made some progress.

Mr. Speaker, in my turn, I wish to pay hommage to you as Speaker of this House and add my good wishes to those of my colleagues.

May I ask you to extend my sincere congratulations to the Deputy Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) and the officers of the House, and I am not forgetting the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lamoureux).

As a newcomer to parliamentary life, and if the old-timers do not scorn too much such newcomers as myself, perhaps they will be interested in the naive observations of a woman who has yet to get used to the rather belligerent games which honorable members at times allow themselves to play. I was rather flabbergasted, during last week's debate on the resolution for peace in Viet Nam, by the calm assertion of the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) that women brought about the war in Vietnam just as they did many other wars. To my mind, if some would reflect on belligerence, which the dictionary defines as the love of war, they have a subject of reflection right at hand.
Indeed, instead of taking the House as the voters have seen fit to return it, and of making the best of it to govern the country, some members of the opposition, it seems to me, have nothing better to do than to seek to prove that this chamber is not perfect. Are we to believe that the Progressive Conservatives have invented new mathematics to reduce a value to a lower one?
As a neophyte, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that I feel closer to the simple Canadian citizen. I share the psychology of the man on the street rather than the habits and traditions of this very sophisticated assembly. I wish we would be practical. I wish we could leave aside sterile disputes and artificial debates in order to work for the betterment of the Canadian society in terms of social justice and economic prosperity.
The Address-Miss Begin

In fact, all that work has to be done: administer $31 billion and manage a country that is young, vast and complex, on behalf of 21.5 million inhabitants. The office of Member of Parliament is not, as I have often heard it described, a more or less honorary one. It is a full-time job, with no overtime pay. I have the honour and the weighty responsibility to represent here the most densely populated riding in Quebec, the riding of Saint-Michel, for the sole purpose of participating in that work.
The men and women I represent here, Mr. Speaker, are ordinary people. I represent 150,000 of them. Some came to lose themselves in the anonymity of a big city from different parts of the province of Quebec. Others came from the heart of Montreal, pushing a little more to the north-east, and tens of thousands of others came and are still coming from Southern Europe and about every part of the world, to build a future for themselves and their families in Canada. They are those to whom I must render some account and they will not be satisfied with words. Concrete action will be necessary to prove to them that the $18 million paid each year by the treasury to enable Parliament to operate really serve the taxpayers. This is the joint responsibility and the work of each and every member.
In the legislative program proposed in the Speech from the Throne, the constituents of Sa int-Michel will be pleased to note a number of correcti ves and improvements or new programs which answer their concern and their idea of a more just society where parents hope their children will be happy. Needless to say, I fully approve the two prime objectives stated in the Speech from the Throne. As a new member, allow me to point out in the second part of my speech certain points which seem important to me and about which I would like to make the following comments. I do not deny the extent of the economic problems; many of my colleagues have talked about them, and as we work as a team, I will talk about other matters.
The views of constituents of all ages about national unity have particularly impressed me during the many meetings and discussions of my first election campaign. The search and the need for a feeling of national unity are undeniable. Complaints of lack of tolerance and, indeed, of friendship between the various communities comprising our country, were voiced many, many times. But I do not despair about our common futu re, because I also witnessed in my constituency amazing examples of true mutual help.
Ignorance and fear of the unknown are at the root of many misunderstandings which sometimes degenerate into fierce struggles and shame us. Many exchange and work group programs for young people are now offered by various departments which allow for the formation of personal ties of friendship between the French and English communities in Canada.
But what better than radio and television can give each individual the idea of what he is, the wish to exist by himself and the emotion of having things in common? You may think that it is futile to refer to this paragraph in particular of the Speech from the Throne announcing a national communications policy. I do not think so because

January 15, 1973
The Address-Miss Begin
I know, as do many other citizens, that the messages that wash over us, a little more each day, from the mass media, as they are called, have unsuspected consequences for the future of the country. Radio and television programs affect us in a sly way which we cannot control. For instance, everyone talks about pollution. Lakes, rivers, forests, towns, the air, everything is polluted, but what about mental pollution? Like the other forms of pollution, it is involuntary; it seems to be an unfortunate result of our economic production system of maximum profit at minimum cost. Two efforts appear to be urgent in the broadcasting industry: first, a coordinated effort to develop Canadian creative talent in all areas-records, books, films, the theater-that supply broadcasting as an industry which is worth $1.2 billion by a conservative estimate, and second, an effort to define responsibility to the public as regards freedom of expression. We in Canada are proud to treat freedom of expression with the greatest of respects but the people cannot accept this to be a one-way privilege. In other words, Canadians have access to an ever-increasing number of programs, but what is being offered to them?
We could, for instance, show them the House in action. But enough of this impertinence! I would now like to say, in passing, a word about showing our debates on television. Canadians might get the impression of taking a more active part in the federal government if they knew more about its machinery, and televising parliamentary proceedings would no doubt help to reach that objective.

Anxieties about the broadcasting of parliamentary proceedings fall into two categories. The first is that broadcasting will indirectly affect the internal functioning of parliament, and the second is that it will alter the relationship between parliament and the people. But the whole weight of experience in other countries shows these fears to be groundless. It is probably significant that no legislature, having once permitted broadcasting of its proceedings, has permanently abandoned the practice.
As Anthony Wedgewood Benn once remarked about the British legislature, "Parliament is either the grand forum of the nation, or it is nothing at all." The business of this grand forum is the public's business, and should be as widely known as possible.

But voices are still missing, so it seems to me, in this great forum of the nation: those of one third of the people of this country whose mother tongue is neither French nor English and who, often, have come from other countries with a cultural heritage of a particular richness and colour.
Dos Passos said, and I quote:
You can tear a man away from his country, but you cannot tear his country out of a man's heart.
I really wish, Mr. Speaker, that the multiculturalism policy, in a bilingual context, as introduced in this House on October 8, 1971 by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), will bring about the development of more community or cultural projects from which all Canadians could benefit.
National unity could not be better achieved than through real efforts to provide equal opportunities for all

Canadians. Let me comment now on three points of the social policy as proposed by this government. I must admit that I shall speak here as a wonoian member of this House. Moreover, I am proud to be the first Quebec woman to take the floor in the House of Commons since the advent of Confederation. This will certainly bring a smile on the lips of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacin-the-he ran away, he is no longer here-who unfortunately voiced-everybody remembers it-on Oc'	4, 1972-
not 1872-in Rimouski, his deep concern about seeing a "woman being appointed minister or Member of Parliament". "She must stay-he said-with her children; her role is within the family". Let us speak then about the family, not through old line and barren cliches, but in the context of everyday's life events.
The guaranteed annual income for all is undoubtedly the dream of many people. As for its achievement-as far as cost and implementation are concerned-it is another problem. It will be introduced, during the 29th Parliament, in favour of, and I quote:
... people who cannot work . ..
Special mention is made for the blind, the aged and the disabled. Now, the most striking feature arising from the hearings and research held by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada is that the poorest among the poorest, in Canada are women. And the most vulnerable are undoubtedly women who are heads of families- widows, divorced, separated, abandoned women or unmarried mothers. If they decide to work, they often find it difficult to get a suitable salary since they generally have no or little vocational training or not enough education. Anyway, our society is not organized for them nor to assist them in the care of their children. The only solution to the dramatic problems of that group is a guaranteed annual income. Obviously, the same should be done for men alone who have dependent children and who are low wage earners. The traditional social organization allowed the families to "retrieve"-for want of a better word-the costs and hardships that they had imposed upon themselves to raise children because these integrated themselves relatively quickly into the family production system, be it on the farm, in trade or in the small entre-prise. Particularly at the time when couples have yet to make any savings today's society imposes unlimited costs for parents whose children have left them very often before they had become productive. And they begin to earn money at the same time as they are getting married. This means that a ceiling, either direct or indirect, situat-

ed around $10,000 does not recognize society's responsibility towards the renewal of its own foundations. It seems to me that a family allowance system should be a part of a universal social security plan which should not be confused with measures intended to fight poverty.

Mr. Speaker, as a new member I noticed that there is always one area of quiet, dignified and gracious sanity in the House, and I would like first to give my commendation to those in the Speaker's Chair who make it so.
We in the Progressive Conservative party had hoped that by now this parliament would be attending to the problems of Canada with specific legislative proposals. Many of my constituents in York East are retired or semi-retired and live on fixed incomes, particularly in the borough of East York. I am acutely aware of their needs and had hoped that we could get on with help for our first citizens as our first business. The Liberals, NDP and Creditistes did not agree to our proposal last week that the debate on the Speech from the Throne be adjourned so that the House could immediately deal with such needs as an increase in the old age pension.
However, the continuation of the debate on the Speech from the Throne does give me an opportunity to say some things I would not otherwise have the opportunity to say. Those things which distinguish my riding are, the personalities who live there and the sense of community which still prevails despite our location within the giant megalopolis known as metro Toronto. The man who today more than any other in Canada personifies individualism, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbak-er), was a resident of the area I now represent in 1901, 1902 and 1903. The right hon. member's father, William
The Address-Mr. Arrol
Diefenbaker, was the principal of the one room local school in what was then the village of Todmorden. One of those who was a pupil of William Diefenbaker was R. H. McGregor who was to represent York East in the parliament of Canada for close to three decades until 1962. In 1972, the electors of York East decided to return to the faith of their fathers, and so today I find myself in parliament, a parliament where the dominant mood is, as it is in the country as a whole, a desire to cope with bread and butter issues.
I would like to observe, however, that even if all the economic problems of Canada could be solved at this session to the general satisfaction of most parties, there would still remain an unease in the land which has as its basis the fact that we do not know collectively what it means to be a Canadian. We as a nation suffer from what theologian Reinhold Niebuhr diagnosed as the general malaise of youth today-an unfocussed craving for affirmation. Despite our advancements in the economic and cultural fields, there is still this strange unease in the land, an unease which can probably only be settled through some project to which all Canadians can give their adherence and thus build up a sense of Canadianism. We will not create a healthy Canadianism on the foundation of criticizing our neighbours. We cannot effectively tell Russia what she should do, nor the U.S. what she should do, nor yet China or Britain. All we can effectively do as Canadians is to propose something that Canada can do.
I propose as a matter for discussion, as a possibility for the future, that in the name of peace, a field in which Canada has already made such significant contributions, Canada give up the right to use its armed forces for any national purpose whatsoever. Let one nation seek to establish peace by preparing absolutely for peace instead of preparing for war. Today in the name of truth, justice, honour, brotherhood and peace, each nation seeks to establish these ideals, and principally the ideal of peace, by preparing for war. Today, in the name of all that is most sacred, the big nations of the world are prepared collectively to kill off everybody-three billion people-in the matter of a few hours. Any survivors would have a horror worse than immediate death.
The world's only salvation may be a reconstituted and strengthened United Nations with the power to keep the peace between nations. And the only way the United Nations can be renewed, reconstituted and given the power to put its ideals into effect may be by a dramatic initiative by one nation. We could take a step all by ourselves, then invite other nations to join us in the name of humanity the world over.
Let us put the ideals of the United Nations-to which all nations say they subscribe-into practice, step by step, nation by nation, starting with Canada. This would be our affirmation, our cause, our way of asserting ourselves nationally in the service of an ideal that would go beyond our national borders, that would make us masters in our own house, subject to no other nation's foreign policy, but in service to all: I declare for peace, and I would have my nation so declare. I affirm that the use of armed force in the world is a world responsibility, and not that of any one nation. To this end, I ask of my government that the

The Address-Mr. Arrol
Department of National Defence be superseded and that in its place be instituted the Department for United Nations Co-operation. I ask that Canada immediately give up its right to use armed forces in aid of or against any other country in any manner whatsoever, unless at the direction of the United Nations.
We could invite the United Nations to pass a resolution to this effect: that whereas Canada has renounced forever the right to command unilaterally the use of her arms, the United Nations set up a peace force and an inspection system to effect the dismantling of all war-making potential in Canada, except that sanctioned by the United Nations, and to ascertain for the future that Canada has kept her pledge. The United Nations inspection force for Canadian disarmament will also be empowered, through the agency of the International Court of Justice, to inspect all treaties which may now be in effect or which might be initiated in the future to which Canada is signatory, to ensure that no treaty with other nations shall in any way obligate the nation to any warlike act under any circumstances. This would give an opportunity for the United Nations to function: Canada would be a laboratory for the development of United Nations peacekeeping functions. Canada could invite other nations to make a similar declaration and offer similar co-operation. Such Canadian action could offer an alternative to fear in the world.
While Communism would remain a menace, it has, in some countries which are still developing, provided the crusading initiative necessary to get into the twentieth century. Put another way, Communism inspires backward nations to pull themselves up by their own bootstraps. When a have-not nation becomes a have-nation, and this includes Communist countries, its basic self interest is for economic advancement, for trading goods and not ideas. It is mainly because the world is an armed camp, and each and every nation feels insecure, that the competition is more in ideology than in trade.
Communism, as we all know, survives best in a climate of hunger and unfulfilled national objectives of underdeveloped countries. The best antidote to Communism would be assistance by the United Nations, through the United Nations, for a united campaign against the common enemies of hunger and disease. To help bring about that ideal, we in Canada, through instituting a Department for United Nations Co-operation in place of a war department, could immediately launch an economic program for the underdeveloped nations of the world.
Canada could launch what eastern Canadian educator Alastair M. Taylor referred to a number of years ago as "A Peacetime British Commonwealth Air Training Plan". Mr. Taylor points out that the Air Training Plan graduated 113,553 airmen during its war years of operation at a cost of $1,281,000,000. The Department of National Defence now spends more in one year than was spent during all the years of the operation of the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan. A peacetime British Commonwealth air training plan could be a project lasting perhaps five years under which Canada would invite people from underdeveloped nations for special training in medicine, agriculture and industrial techniques. Apart from China, Southeast Asia and the Latin American countries, most other underdeveloped nations have as

their national language French or English and Canada is bilingual.
This project shared by French and English speaking Canadians could have unifying qualities for Canada, drawing us together as we united the visiting nations on our soil in this educational undertaking. We could invite research scientists from other countries to join us in educational projects; scientists and technicians who would like to work for a constructive projeclt instead of those for destruction. And as we developed instructors and facilities for this co-operative endeavour, we would be providing for our own industrial and trade expansion, although the basic idea would be a practical working out of United Nations ideals.
In many other ways Canada could be a laboratory, a workshop, a showcase for United Nations purposes. We could invite the United Nations to orga nize an inspection team for Arctic protection, to see that no Russian or United States or any other nation's missile-carrying submarines used our northwest passage, there to lurk under the ice and on an appropriate occasion blast through and release a missile. We could dismantle the Distant Early Warning System set up by the Americans in northern Canada-or we could make the system available to the United Nations, with inspectors looking south as well as north. We could even provide a few thousand square miles of our northern territory for experiments in the detection of underground nuclear explosions. We could make available our soil, our air space, our waters, as we made available our determination to do all in our power to bring peace on earth.
If Canada were to take a separate path from the other western nations, we of course would be opposed. A Canadian resolve to give up its right to use its armed forces for any national purpose whatssoe'ver, and to put our military at the disposal of the Uni1 :ed Nations through a Department for United Nations Co-operation, would take as much courage as going to war. It would indeed be the moral equivalent of going to war. But no matter what the price, we would have chartered the cou rse for no less than a Made-in-Canada Declaration of Inde pendence. It is ideals and not economic warfare which call forth a nation to life, to spirit. We would be opposed, but in being opposed our character would be strengthened. We would have a cause in Canada, a crusade which could unite the nation.
The Indians under Gandhi practised non-violence for the independence of their nation; the Negroes under Martin Luther King for recognition of a race. Our task would be non-violence for the recognition and fulfillment of the possibilities for good in all mankind,, a first practical step to peace on earth. Some nation at some time soon must act as a catalyst to break the armed camps in which the nations of the world find themselves today; some nation must cause a revolution in thinking about war and its inevitability. I have suggested a course for Canada which I hope this House and the country will consider. It may be such a course could be a significant step towards our salvation and the world's.

Mr. Speaker, my opening words are to congratulate you on your success in the Stormont-Dundas constituency and on your re-election to the office of House Speaker. In the course of the twenty-eighth parliament, you won the admiration of all hon. members.

I should like also to welcome the four new members representing the female element, that is the Minister of State for Science and Technology and member for Ahunt-sic (Mrs. Sauve), the hon. member for Saint-Michel (Miss Begin), the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) and the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald).
To begin with and on the occasion of the opening of this twenty-ninth Parliament, I should like to make a few remarks on the man in public life and on Parliament and its importance.
Politics should be the concern of respectable men and women, aiming at using their mind and their skills to erect a city, a province, a country where peace and prosperity might prevail. Participation in the political life is a duty that social justice dictates, since every citizen must contribute as much as possible to the common good of his country.
The politician, because of his role and his duties, has always occupied a useful place within society, for, through his oath of office, he has chosen to serve this society, to work for the common good. There is need to create a public opinion which, without looking for scandal, will expose frankly and courageously persons and circumstances working against the law and the purposes of institutions.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the basic principles on which rest my short political life. The application of these principles allowed me to gain the confidence of 29,000 voters during the election of last October 30, in the constituency of Laval. I consider this responsibility not as a member of Parliament but rather as a citizen at the service of the constituency of Laval, and at the service of Canada. I agreed to serve my constituency, to defend the interests of my province and to work for the good of my country while contributing to improve the standard of living of Canadians and learning to better know the needs of the Canadian family, the various ethnic groups and the various social levels represented in all classes of our society.
Since my election of June 25, 1968 I have changed some of my views about Parliament which I considered a rather out of date and inefficient institution. Having been a member since then and participated in the exercise of democracy in this House or as a committee member, I have come to better understand the nature and role of this

institution. Perhaps it is a normal beginner's reaction and probably the 100 new members will also have the same reaction. In spite of weaknesses that nobody denies Parliament is still the best system of government in this world even though it lends itself to criticism and could be improved upon.

I am sometimes under the impression that we do not realize all the advantages we are enjoying. There are on earth every possible kind of government but I doubt that many Canadians would agree to exchange their own system of government for that of many other foreign countries where severe restrictions are imposed on people speaking too frankly and where political opponents are put into jail.
Even though sometimes Pamliament seems to move away from the people or people seem to lose interest in this institution let there be a crisis and they look to Parliament to act for the good of the country.

I thought I should present tl lose observations at the outset of this 29th Parliament which includes more than 100 new members.

ment for its failure to take action about the problems of unemployment and I wonder whether he is not really furthering his own ambitions at the expense of the unemployed.

The relative growth of the labour force in Canada during those six years was almost 20 times that of all 15 major industrialized European countries, twice that of Japan and 58 per cent higher than that of the United States which ranks second in the world for the growth rate of its labour force.
What was the increase in the number of jobs? There were 1,300,000 new jobs created in Canada between 1965 and 1970. The increase in the number of jobs in Canada was 400,000, 50 per cent more than the real increase in the number of jobs in all the 15 major industrialized European countries and 505,000, or 66 per cent more than the total increase in the number of jobs in the seven major European countries, i.e. Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Sweden and the Netherlands.
The relative rate of increase in the number of jobs in Canada was 50 per cent higher than in the United States, twice higher than in Japan, 7J times higher than in Germany and 27 times higher than in all those 15 European countries.
During the years 1970 and 1971 the relative rate of increase in the number of jobs in Canada was three times higher than the corresponding rate in the United States.
Those figures are evidence of the extent to which the Liberal government concentrated on the problem of unemployment through various programs implemented, by the creation of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to create employment in areas where industries were not functioning normally, by the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and also by the economic incentives offered by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
