I have attempted to constructively place before this House proposals to improv e the way of life of all those who live in the Atlantic provinces. Whether these or better suggestions are acted upon is not important. What is important is that we act decisively, and now.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker,
in opening my remarks I should like to congratulate you on your re-election to this House, and to join those hon. members who during the course of the debate have paid well deserved tribute to your wisdom, fairness and many other skills. I am both proud and happy that you have been enthusiastically, and indeed unanimously selected again to guide the proceedings of this chamber during the twenty-ninth parliament. I congratulate the Deputy Speaker on his election, and I also congratulate, for their excellent performances, the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I recall vividly my emotions, my excitement and feelings of humility, mixed with great satisfaction, when in 1957 I arrived in this House for the first time. Today, my feelings are no less intense. I stand here again with mixed feelings of humility and pride as the first Minister of State whose sole responsibility it is to implement and develop further the multicultural policy of the government.
You had better do a good job, Stanley.

To these feelings I have to add, in all sincerity, my sense of gratitude to my parents, who immigrated to Canada from Poland many years ago, for their hard work, privations and guidance without which I would not have completed my education nor succeeded im my chosen career, to my teachers and friends in Toronto where I was born and educated, to my professors at the University of Ottawa, to the constituents of my multicultural riding of Parkdale for the clear mandate with which they sent me back to this House, and to the community of which I am a proud member, for their encouragement to enter into and to continue a role in the political life of this country.
I was deeply touched, Sir, by the reaction with which my appointment was greeted by the various ethnocultural communities across the country and their periodicals which, although in languages other than English or French are, nevertheless, Canadian in spirit. I was not surprised, of course, by the expression of warm, proud satisfaction by the Polish-Canadian press. I was, however, greatly moved by the sincere, spontaneous statements and congratulations flowing from other ethnocultural groups.
I am grateful for their kindness and assure them of my continued support and receptiveness to their advice on how I and my dedicated officials can improve the efforts which have already begun in giving multiculturalism genuine substance in Canada.
All of us here are sensitive to the needs of ethnic groups and the richness they add to Canadian society, because the multicultural policy received support from all parties when it was announced by our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on October 8, 1971.

All we want is more money.

January 15, 1973
The Address-Mr. Haidasz

I rejoice at the enthusiastic response to this policy from all ethnocultural groups. It is a fitting testimony to the viability of the multicultural policy of the government and an example of the integrating spirit and natural adoptive forces of our country, where mistrust can be shed in a cordial atmosphere of mutual trust, replaced by togetherness and understanding directed toward a brighter future, and by preservation of what is best in the past. Without it, multiculturalism would remain only a beautiful theory.
The appointment of a minister of state responsible for multiculturalism illustrates the positive influence of the philosophical and moral basis of the policy of multiculturalism. How right was the Prime Minister, when announcing this policy on October 8, 1971, he said in his memorable statement on that historic occasion:
A policy of multiculturalism within a bilingual framework commends itself to the government as the most suitable means of assuring the cultural freedom of Canadians. Such a policy should help to break down discriminatory attitudes and cultural jealousies.
Where is the advisory board?

National unity, if it is to mean anything in the deeply personal sense, must be founded on confidence in one's own individual identity; out of this can grow respect for that of others and a willingness to share ideas, attitudes and assumptions. A vigorous policy of multiculturalism will help create this initial confidence. It can form the base of a society which is based on fair play for all.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, fair play for all is the principle guiding the implementation of this policy as outlined in the Prime Minister's document. I have not the least doubt that when the history of this time in our country's affairs is written, the Prime Minister's statement, making manifest his government's determination to provide all ethnocultural groups with a sense of belonging without first having to sacrifice their cultural heritage, will be regarded as one of the truly enlightened and just policies adopted by any administration.
You don't believe that.

During the past 14 months of implementation, the citizenship branch of the Department of the Secretary of State and the federal cultural agencies have done an impressive job to launch new programs and to develop those which had already existed. It was only in January of last year, hardly a year ago, that $3 million were made available for the fiscal period ending March, 1973, to finance the initial stages of all these programs. The best known of these is the one for various cultural projects proposed and carried out by the cultural and ethnic groups themselves. Until now, out of $1 million earmarked for them, the citizenship branch has assisted a total of 229 projects with grants amounting to $826,772. Another granting session will commence next week.
These grants cover a wide range of activities, from traditional dance and song ensembles and other manifestations of folklore, to cable-TV presentations, anthologies of ethnic prose and poems written in Canada and published in English and French, theatrical performances, bibliographies of Canadian ethnic material, exhibitions and imaginative multicultural ventures in which many

groups participate, including English and French speaking.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, if I were to cite the assistance which has been provided to various groups some better understanding of the government's role in promoting multiculturalism may be obtained. For example, the Estonian Canadians were assisted in staging an impressive world festival of their culture in Toronto last summer. Similar festivals, although on a smaller scale, were organized, with federal support, by Latvians in Vancouver and Lithuanians in Montreal.
A prominent Czech writer received a grant to enable him to publish, in French, his Czech novel depicting integration of an immigrant intellectual into the French-Canadian milieu in Montreal. A Hungarian researcher was helped in publishing, in English, a bibliography of Hungarian, English and French publications pertaining to Hungary and Hungarian Canadians. A number of amateur theatrical groups, Jewish, Latvian, Polish, Ukrainian, and others, in Montreal, Toronto and Edmonton were assisted in their productions. The East Indian community in Vancouver received help to present a Sikh cultural variety program which later toured other centres in British Columbia. Another grant enabled the Korean group to present their culture, modern and classical music, dance and theatre to the Toronto public.
A multi-ethnic group in remote Rouyn-Noranda received assistance to help their members to maintain their languages and cultures. A Cape Breton youth group, consisting of members of 11 racial strains, used a grant awarded by the citizenship branch to learn more about their own cultural heritage and to share this knowledge with other members of the community. In the same area, a Lebanese Canadian women's group received a grant to save the art of Lebanese cuisine and other homemaking traditions from disappearing. In another project, assisted by multicultural funds, two Montreal youth groups, Polish and French-Canadian, have been getting together to share each other's culture, concentrating on songs and dances. Although the project has not yet been completed, it has already yielded some happy results. The Polish group raised additional funds themselves to visit their country of origin last summer, and while performing there in an international festival won a coveted prize for their rendition of French-Canadian dances.
There have been numerous other projects, special conferences, colloquia and festivals, German, black, Maltese, Greek, Ukrainian, and many others. A particularly successful festival was the one held in St. Thomas, Ontario, where the grant received was minimal in proportion to the enthusiasm and spontaneous participation of the whole community which is proud of its multicultural heritage.
The Canadian past was also remembered and honoured. A grant to the Jewish Historical Society of western Canada was instrumental in organizing an impressive multi-media exhibition on "The History of the Jews in Western Canada" which opened in Winnipeg late last year. I saw this exhibit and found it most interesting and well presented. The one-hundredth anniversary of the settlement of the Danes in New Brunswick benefited from

this granting program when the community of New Denmark celebrated their centennial. The German-speaking Amish Mennonites were the focus of attention when the Mennonite Historical Society of Ontario organized a series of uplifting celebrations to commemorate 150 years of the settlement of the Old Order of Amish in southern Ontario. Part of their commemoration, an oratorio which was presented in the Avon Theatre at Stratford, was assisted by a multicultural grant.
I believe the examples I have cited prove the viability of this government's policy to assist in the preservation and development of our cultural riches and to promote better understanding among Canadians. But in addition to the granting program there are other undertakings which are equally important. An extensive research program is being undertaken to produce information on language maintenance and cultural development.
Meaningful multiculturalism c tinot ignore this complex problem. If we want to successfully develop programs outlined in the House document tabled by the Prime Minister, we have to understand all the linguistic and cultural phenomena. Some ethnic groups, those who manifest a "collective will to exist" as the B and B Commission had termed it, attach utmost importance to the retention of their languages, as witnessed by the considerable number of their evenings and Saturdays language schools. To other groups, language is of less importance. A special study is now in progress in Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Edmonton and Vancouver involving some of the largest ethnocultural groups. I hope that this study, which should be completed by late summer, will yield enough data to enable the government to assess where its further support could most effectively be directed.
I wish to stress, Mr. Speaker, this government's interest in the important role of Canadian ethnic publications. A great deal has already been done to assist them in carrying out their role, and even more will be done in the future. A part of the research program of our multicultural policy which I have just mentioned deals with the many problems of the ethnic press. The postal tariffs and insufficient income from advertising are not the only malaise which affects the many ethnic and other periodicals. There are many other factors, both internal and external, which also affect their content, readership, circulation, advertising, distribution and delivery and other operating costs.
While there are some papers which are self-sufficient, there are many others unable to solve their financial and other difficulties. Some of these were considered by the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism and by the special Senate Committee on Mass Media, and others. Our study should give a comprehensive picture as to which ethnic publishers and editors will contribute individually or through their Canada Ethnic Press Federation and its affiliate clubs in Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver, thus enabling the government to undertake proper measures. I would like to stress, however, that it is unlikely that the government would consider measures which would not also apply to ailing community weeklies across the country whose plight is very similar.
The Address-Mr. Haidasz
Under another program we have commissioned the writing of 20 ethnic histories by academics familiar with their respective groups. The purpose of this series on the peoples of Canada is to acquaint Canadians better with each other, to demonstrate that all groups have contributed to the growth and development of Canada's economic, social, cultural and political life. So far, contracts have been signed for 15 histories. The first volume will appear this year and the rest will be completed over the next three years. The problem of Canadian ethnic studies is also under consideration and prominent Canadian scholars are being consulted on the feasibility of establishing special centres of ethnic studies.
Mention should be made of multicultural centres where members of all groups can meet and share their cultural experiences and heritages. The only centres which have received substantial assistance to date a.re the International Institute of Metropolitan Toronto, L'Accord in Montreal, and the International Centre of Winnipeg. All three are considerably involved in immigrant-orientation work. There are, however, many smaller communities interested in the creation of multicultural centres, although on a smaller scale. Groups in such places are encouraged and assisted in their feasibility studies and preparation of suitable plans.
Four federal cultural agencies, apart from the citizenship branch of the Department of Secretary of State, are involved in the implementation of the multicultural policy and have their own programs. The National Film Board is making a series of films on ethnic groups. What is particularly important about these films is that they depart from the usual concept of folklore and depict the life of Canadians of ethnic groups, as it is lived today, among all other Canadians. The National Film Board has also completed extensive research preparatory to the launching of a program to show versions of existing films in other languages and distribute them to ethnic groups across Canada.
The National Museum of Man has created and put on tour two special exhibitions on ethnic groups in Canada and is developing its collection of multicultural artifacts. The public archives and the national library are also building up their collection of historical and current material relating to ethnic groups in our country. The CRTC is also involved. It has under way at the present time a major study on the use of other languages and is carrying out research of its own on ethnic broadcasting. The CBC has had a special committee studying the way in which that corporation can contribute to the realization of multicultural objectives and I hope it will be reporting to its president very shortly.
I regret that time does not permit me to describe all the multicultural programs of the federal government's cultural agencies in more detail, but there will be other opportunities to do so. At this time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress the spirit of co-operation and consultation underlying the formulation and implementation of the multicultural policy. All the programs I have mentioned were not conceived in an ivory tower; they were preceded by countless discussions and consultations between federal and provincial agencies, communities and groups they are to serve. My predecessors in the Department of Secre-

I am sure that the government will be fully supported in its measures to give effect to its programs implementing multiculturalism and to develop its policies further in light of the needs and desires of our ethnocultural groups.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that the government's agenda for action outlined in the Speech from the Throne contains many remedies to solve our socioeconomic problems and to improve the quality of life for all our citizens. Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate you quite sincerely for having been unanimously re-elected as Speaker of this House.
I was very pleased in recent years to take part in the proceedings under your speakership because you have always treated all members with much fairness and generosity. It happened sometimes, especially in my case, that we have unwillingly violated our standing orders-
Often.

Someone said often but I know that he is joking. In all honesty he knows quite well that I have always tried, as do my colleagues, to respect the authority of the Speaker.
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) is nodding yes because he knows that I am telling the truth.
I should also like to congratulate the Deputy Speaker for his election. He has truly deserved the confidence of the House and I am convinced that we shall be able to count on his understanding and generosity so that the proceedings of the House may be truly efficient.

Also, I would like, at the beginning of my remarks, to thank very sincerily the voters of the riding of Bellechasse who have re-elected me at the last election and this despite pressure from promises and without hopes for a big election fund because third parties are without these advantages.
I should also like to say a word of praise for my chief, although he is not here now, because of his brave speech in the House last Monday when he took part on the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. He kindly outlined what, during the coming weeks and months, will be the position of our party with regard to administration and to the debates in the House. I am particularly anxious to tell him and the whole nation how much I respect him for having used the same language both in the east and in the west of the country when addressing the Canadian people. It is a well-deserved homage and I must sincerely say honight with pride that he is a great Canadian, a sincere Canadian and that of course the whole of Canada must recognize him as such.
Mr. Speaker, I also want to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for having, during the last election campaign, visited the riding of Bellechasse which I represent. The right hon. Prime Minister has honoured me by his presence and I am convinced that he has done so as Prime Minister and not as a party leader; I must pay him tribute for that.
I must also thank the numerous ministers who paid me a visit during the electoral campaign. In all the areas where these ministers visited the Bellechasse population, my plurality has been increased; so, I invite them to come back again when the opportunity arises.
Many federal and provincial Liberal members also paid me a visit. Mr. Speaker, it is useless to say that on each and every occasion these hon. members did not ask the population to vote for me. They simply said to the people that if they wanted to be well represented, they should vote on the "right side".
Mr. Speaker, people from Bellechasse did indeed vote for the right side because they voted for a member representing the population first rather than a party's interests, for somebody who took the situation seriously and who, under any circumstances, can stand up and do his utmost to make the voice of the population heard within these precincts.
Mr. Speaker, of course if all Canadians had voted for the right side as many said, it would have meant voting for the Liberal party and there would not have been any opposition. One could imagine the ensuing disaster.
Mr. Speaker, I see the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Corriveau) applauding warmly. Yet I must say that he came to my riding and told the farmers: You know nothing about farming, but I do. I am a guy who climbs telephone and telegraph poles. I know about farming. In fact, he said this in Sainte-Germaine-de-Bellechasse: It is pointless for you to have stables and expensive buildings, you know nothing about them.
Mr. Speaker, during the election campaign we seriously proposed to the people right across Canada, and notably
January 15, 1973

to those of the riding I represent, one single program based on the interests of each and everyone, the respect for human beings, family rights and the individual citizen. We wanted to introduce an honest program in order to bring about improvements.
Mr. Speaker, I was saying a few moments ago that my friends came to my riding and told people to vote "for the right side", meaning for the party in power, but at that time, nobody knew who would form the government. Was it to be a minority government or a majority government, would it be formed by my friends the Progressive Conservatives, by my friends the Liberals, by my friends the New Democrats or by the Social Credit party? The situation was so uncertain that no one could predict what was going to happen.
It was a question of voting for the "right side", according to one's conscience, to send to this Parliament members who would form this democratic assembly.
On October 30, 264 members were elected. Such was the responsibility of the people: to elect 264 parliamentarians to form the assembly of the nation. And now, we, the parliamentarians, must assume a very big responsibility in legislating for the common good. For once, parliament will have to be the supreme authority in this country, instead of submitting to the pressures of the executive. This executive, Liberal, Progressive Conservative, NDP or Creditiste, will have to carry out parliament's will. That is how I understand the role of a truly responsible parliament.
I am very happy to have been elected as a member of this House, which will eventually have to account to the people for its actions.
Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to the speeches delivered by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), and all the other members who had the courage to express their views in this House, and I was most interested to find that we all have the same purpose: To give our country the best administration possible.
Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned, I am not here to indulge in politicking, to overthrow the government at every occasion, but to work with all the members of this House and pass any legislation required to reform what must be reformed in order to give justice to our senior citizens, our mothers, our handicaped and our children.
Mr. Speaker, we have often had the opportunity in this Parliament to propose measures having the same objective as the one referred to in the current Speech from the Throne. Personally, I am happy to see that finally wisdom seems to have caught the heart of the Prime Minister.
I remember, Mr. Speaker, that when I sat to your left, I used to say the same things as now and people used to laugh at me. There was even a minister who visited my constituency and made references to those people who thought along the same lines as Major Douglas, who had recommended financial reforms designed to ensure justice and liberty for all. The minister who is here tonight said: "All those who believe in the Social Credit party are psychiatric cases."
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
Let us think, Mr. Speaker, about ho w many psychiatric cases exist in Canada since October 30: more than 750,000 voters, and their number increases every day. I say that those who let men, women and children live in suffering and misery, in a country of abundance are more in need of psychiatric care than those who take steps to ensure a fair distribution of resources deveL oped by Canadians for all Canadians. I am here tonight to defend those people and speak on their behalf so that, all together, as members of Parliament, leaving aside our political views, we can work to enact as soon as possible legislation in line with Canadian possibilities.
I also witnessed, Mr. Speaker, during this debate, quarrels, unjustified charges, which were hurled from both sides of this House, between French and English-speaking members. We are Canadians first, we live in a vast country full of resources of all kinds, and our people, full of energy, are quite prepared to transform all these resources so that all of us can benefit from them!
Mr. Speaker, I have here a report published by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce of the province of Quebec, which is very recent, and I believe that those who published the figures I will quote are just as honest as we are, so that we can trust them. This report states that the gross national product of the province of Quebec, in 1972, amounted to $25 billion, while personal income, in the same province, for the same period totalled $20 billion. This means, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians who live in Quebec did the best they could in order to produce in their province everyting that was possible for the benefit of the population.
I will quote from a report for the information of my English-speaking friends who blamed severely the former Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) for having done too much for the province of Quebec. We can say things among ourselves without hurting one another and examine the situation. I quote:
To be on the right side you have to be on the Liberal side, and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion has given everything to the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, in 1972, the rate of unemployment in the province of Quebec was the highest in Canada; according to the report I have here it stood at 8.3 per cent. If that means being partial to a province at the expense of the others, distributive justice and administrative honesty do not make any sense to me anymore. A nd I will have to tell my Liberal friends that if in order to vote the "right way" one must vote Liberal, they managed well, but they mainly succeeded in giving the province of Quebec the highest rate of unemployment in Cai radian history.
Is that voting the "right way"? I do not think so. I think that voting the "right way" is voting for a party that takes steps to put a stop to discrimination in this country and to understand that we must all together reach the objective set for us by the Canadian people on October 30.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne suggests certain reforms that I approve of. It proposes solutions as well as the possibility for Parliament to administer more properly the commonweal and provide for a greater distribution of wealth with greater justice to all citizens.

January 15, 1973
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert However, we will have to look into the bills and analyze them. We will have to examine them from all angles in order to find out whether the government is really putting forward legislative measures in accordance with Canadian possibilities, so that we may reasonably increase the yearly income of the Canadian people, the purchasing power of those who need it, without taking money out of the pockets of those who already have not too much of it, in order to arrive at a certain levelling off in accordance with what has already been desired in other countries.
Mr. Speaker, as regards reforms, the bills that were announced, we should all together greet them with much satisfaction, so as to be able to assess them according to their real merit and to make decisions not in a collective way on the party level, but according to our personal responsibilities. This leads me, Mr. Speaker, to say that I am anxious to see the day when in parliament every member will be called upon to vote freely on any bill after examining it personally without having the party to which he belongs dictate his vote. It is time to change our habits. It is time we stopped voting according to party lines.
I think that in a truly democratic assembly each bill should be assessed on its own value and each member should vote according to his conscience without there being a chance of bringing down the government on it. It is a question of rejecting or passing a piece of legislation and not of approving or condemning a government.
In the Speech from the Throne the government admits I am right when it says it will introduce a bill on capital punishment. He will let each member decide on the bill by a free vote.
Mr. Speaker, if a free vote on capital punishment seems fair, it would also be fair to hold a free vote on the increase in old age pensions, eligibility for pension at 60, family allowances and any other subject. Then we would really be taken seriously by the Canadian people and could provide the best administration Canada ever enjoyed.
I have here an analysis of the 15 general elections held in Canada since May 1925, among which six led to minority governments-
Seven.

Right, seven. And according to the information I also obtained, the best accomplishments of parliament are those of minority governments. Why? Because under a minority government everyone is aware of his responsibilities, of the fact that he should always be where he belongs and seriously study every bill before voting on them.
Such being the case, we could as of tonight carry on in this house truly worthwhile discussions. And I am not saying that for the sake of it. I have twelve dependent children, and as far as they are concerned, I know the consequences of my actions, for I love them as any other father loves his children. Altogether, and discarding partisanship, we want to be in a position to legislate in such a way as to bring high finance to heel.
What does that mean? To my mind it means that high finance has always been in control of Canadian economy

and politics. For once, let the financiers defer to Parliament, just as the unemployed should abide by the Unemployment Insurance Act, the family mother by the Family Allowances Act and the senior citizen by the Old Age Security Act.
I hope that for once the newspapers will report that a member has had the courage to state in this House that high finance and those who control credit should obey the same laws and rules as any other Canadian citizen. This is the only way for us to succeed in giving Canada a truly fair administration that will respect the citizen's rights while respecting the freedom of each and everyone and that will enable us to live as brothers regardless of our language on this great North American territory, to use the huge wealth which Providence put at our disposal and finally enable our sons to live decently instead of remaining unemployed because of a devilish system which prevents them from giving the best of themselves while they are still able to do so. May we finally se e the day when all those young unemployed people, whom we made every sacrifice to have educated, sometimes against their will, but in their best interest, will be accepted in the labour market and will no longer be asked: "Young man, how old are you?" "I am 22." "Do you have experience?" "No, I have just left school." "Well then, go back to school, because here we need experienced people."
Mr. Speaker, if they had waited for you to have the required experience in order to ask you to occupy the high office which is now yours, I believe you would not be there yet, and the same would be true of many of us.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say, in concluding my remarks-and without any reflection on anyone, of course-that I would like this session to be truly efficient and full of confidence. I would like the people to be able to see, and this, on several occasions, that if the members do not seem too serious at times, they know, when the situation becomes serious, how to fulfill their responsibilities, how to forget about partisanship and how to work together in the best interests of Canadian people.
